passages.title: Two paths: nullified deeds and pardoned sins
passages.tafsir:
The surah opens by placing all of humanity into two columns and telling us the final accounting of each: one group whose deeds Allah renders worthless, and another whose sins Allah wipes away and whose whole state He puts right. What holds ayat 1–3 together is that they are a single balanced sentence with a verdict, a counter-verdict, and then — in ayah 3 — the reason behind both. Nothing here is arbitrary: Allah tells us *why* each side ends where it does.

## The surah's other name

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah has a second name, **Sūrah al-Qitāl** — "Surah of war" — because it lays down the rules of jihad and qitāl, that is, armed struggle in the cause of Allah. The surah was revealed immediately after the migration to Madinah, at the point where the ordinances relating to jihad and war were being given.

That is the atmosphere in which these opening ayat land. But notice what ayah 1 actually does before any ruling is issued: it does not begin with a command. It begins with an accounting — a statement about what becomes of two kinds of lives.

## Ayah 1 — two crimes, one verdict

**"Those who disbelieve and hinder (men) from the path of Allah, He will render their deeds vain."**

Ibn Kathir reads the two verbs precisely. *Those who disbelieve* means disbelieve **in the āyāt of Allah** — His signs and His revealed verses. And *hinder* (Arabic **ṣaddū**) he glosses in one word: **others**. So the sentence names two distinct crimes stacked on each other. The first is what a person does to himself: he rejects the signs. The second is what he does to everyone else: he stands in the road and turns people back. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies that "Allah's way" here refers to **Islam** itself — the road, not merely a road.

The verdict on such people is **aḍalla aʿmālahum** — Ibn Kathir explains it as: He renders their deeds **vain and futile, and He denies them any rewards or blessings for them**. Notice the grammar: this is not deeds quietly failing of their own accord. Allah is the one acting on those deeds. Ibn Kathir brings a verse from elsewhere in the Qur'an that pictures it unforgettably — Allah will approach what they have done of deeds "and make them as dispersed dust" (25:23). Not confiscated into a vault. Scattered, like dust in a shaft of light: visible, weightless, unrecoverable.

### The hardest point in the passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on a question the reader is bound to ask. Which deeds, exactly, are rendered vain?

Its answer is unflinching: the phrase **includes actions which are good in themselves** — helping and assisting the destitute, supporting and protecting one's neighbours, generosity, charity, and other good deeds. These acts are genuinely good and righteous *as acts*. But in the Hereafter, such deeds yield benefit **only if blessed with faith**, because faith is a necessary condition for the credibility of good actions. So these righteous deeds will be of no use to the disbeliever in the Hereafter.

That is not a claim that the good was never good. It is a claim about *where it is paid out*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes the picture: the disbelievers **take their comfort in this worldly life as a reward of their good deeds**, and in the Hereafter they are punished with the Fire. The generosity was real; the receipt was cashed here. Faith is what carries a deed across the boundary into the next world — without it, the deed has nowhere to travel to.

Read this with humility rather than as a weapon. The passage explains an accounting principle about the Hereafter; it does not license contempt for the decent, generous unbeliever in front of you. And it turns back on the believer with a sharp edge: if faith is what gives a deed its weight, then the health of your faith is not a private side-matter to your good works — it is the thing that makes them count at all.

## Ayah 2 — four things said about the saved

The counter-verdict is built with unusual care. Ibn Kathir walks through it clause by clause.

**"But those who believe and do righteous good deeds…"** — Ibn Kathir explains that this means **their hearts and souls have believed, and their limbs and their hidden and apparent acts have complied with Allah's Law**. Faith and deeds are not two hobbies. One is the inside, the other the outside, of a single life: the heart assents, and then the body, in what people see and in what they don't, falls into line with what Allah legislated.

**"…and believe in that which is sent down to Muhammad."** Why say this after already saying "those who believe"? Ibn Kathir identifies the device: this is **a method of adding a specific meaning to a general one** — the general statement is made, then one indispensable particular is singled out for emphasis. And he draws the doctrinal conclusion plainly: this **provides proof that after Muhammad's advent, believing in him is a required condition for the true faith**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other side: although the earlier clause already referred to faith that includes the messengership of the Prophet ﷺ and the revelation sent down to him, this clause states explicitly that **the actual basis of faith is to embrace all the teachings of the Last Prophet ﷺ** — all of them, not a selection.

**"…for it is the truth from their Lord."** Ibn Kathir calls this **a beautifully placed parenthetical clause**. The sentence is mid-flight, describing the believers, and Allah interrupts to certify the content of their belief. Their faith is not praised because sincerity is admirable in the abstract; it is praised because the thing they have believed in *is actually true*, and true **from their Lord** — reaching them from the One who is their Master and Sustainer.

### Two gifts

Then the reward, and it is stated in two verbs.

**Kaffara ʿanhum sayyi'ātihim** — "He expiates from them their sins." Ibn Kathir's own paraphrase later in the passage is that Allah **overlooks the sins of the righteous**. Note that the first thing named is not Paradise or reward; it is relief from the record. The believer's sins are not denied — the ayah grants that they have sins — they are wiped away.

**Wa aṣlaḥa bālahum** — "and He amends their *bāl*." This word is hard to render, and the early authorities Ibn Kathir cites each reach for a slightly different English:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: their *matter*.
- **Mujāhid**: their *affair*.
- **Qatādah and Ibn Zayd**: their *condition*.

Ibn Kathir's verdict is that **all of these are similar in meaning** — this is not a dispute so much as four hands feeling the same shape. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further dimension: *bāl* is sometimes used in the sense of one's **state of affairs and condition**, and at other times in the sense of the **heart**, and here it could refer to **both** senses. In the first sense, Allah has set all their affairs aright — their matters of this world and of the Hereafter. In the second, He has improved their hearts. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this has the same implication anyway, since **correction of works is a logical result of improvement of heart**, both being necessary to each other.

So the pairing in ayah 2 is exact. The past is dealt with (sins covered) and the present and future are dealt with (the heart and the whole situation set straight). Forgiveness without repair would leave you where you were; repair without forgiveness would leave the debt standing.

**A word you may already say every day.** Ibn Kathir mentions that this same expression occurs in what has been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ regarding the response given to one who sneezes: *yahdīkumu-llāhu wa yuṣliḥu bālakum* — "May Allah guide you and rectify your *bāl* — your affairs." (Ibn Kathir reports this from the Prophet ﷺ without naming a collection, so we take the teaching without attributing it to a particular book.) It is worth pausing on: a phrase that Allah uses in the Qur'an to describe what He does for the believers is placed on the tongue of ordinary believers as a small daily prayer for one another. You are asking for your brother precisely what ayah 2 promises.

## Ayah 3 — the reason underneath both verdicts

**"That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, while those who believe follow the truth from their Lord."**

Ibn Kathir puts the logic in Allah's own voice: *We only invalidate the deeds of the disbelievers, and overlook the sins of the righteous, and amend their affairs, because those who disbelieve follow falsehood* — meaning, he explains, **they choose falsehood over the truth**.

That word *choose* is the hinge of the whole passage. Both sides in ayah 3 are described by the same verb — **ittabaʿū**, "they followed." The difference is not that one group followed and the other didn't; everyone is following something. The difference is the object: **al-bāṭil**, falsehood, versus **al-ḥaqq min rabbihim**, the truth *from their Lord*. And notice that ayah 3 repeats "from their Lord" for the believers, exactly as ayah 2 did. Their truth has an origin outside themselves; falsehood, by contrast, is named with no source at all.

This is also why the verdict in ayah 1 is just rather than harsh. Deeds scattered like dust are not an arbitrary punishment attached to good acts; ayah 3 tells us plainly what they rest on — a following that was aimed at falsehood from the start.

**"Thus does Allah set forth for mankind their parables."** Ibn Kathir's comment is short and warm: in this way **He makes the consequence of their actions clear to them, and He shows them where they will end in their next life** — and Allah knows best. The passage is not gloating over anyone's ruin. It is a map handed to the reader while there is still time to change roads.

## Living it

- **Check the foundation, not only the output.** Ayah 1 says that real generosity can still come to nothing. Ask not only "what am I doing?" but "what is it resting on?"
- **Faith and limbs together.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 2 — hearts, souls, limbs, hidden and apparent acts — is a checklist. The hidden acts are named alongside the visible ones on purpose.
- **All of the teaching, not a selection.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the basis of faith embracing *all* the teachings of the Last Prophet ﷺ.
- **Ask for the whole gift.** When you seek forgiveness, ask also for *iṣlāḥ al-bāl* — that Allah put your heart and your entire situation right, not only that He cover what is past.
- **Mind what you are following.** Ayah 3 does not ask whether you are following. It asks what.

passages.title: The command to fight and the martyrs' reward
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from the battlefield to the Garden. Ayah 4 gives the believers their instructions for an actual armed encounter — how to fight, what to do with those who fall into their hands afterwards, and why Allah let this struggle happen at all rather than punishing the disbelievers Himself. Then, because war means that believers die, the passage turns to those killed in Allah's way and follows them through ayat 5 and 6 into Paradise.

## "Strike the necks" — the language of a decisive engagement

**فَإِذَا لَقِيتُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ** — "So when you meet those who disbelieve." Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah guiding the believers to what they should employ in their fights against the idolaters.

**فَضَرْبَ ٱلرِّقَابِ** — "smite their necks." Ibn Kathir: "when you fight against them, cut them down totally with your swords."

**حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَثْخَنتُمُوهُمْ** — "until you have fully defeated them." Ibn Kathir explains this to mean: "you have killed and utterly destroyed them."

**فَشُدُّواْ ٱلْوَثَاقَ** — "then tighten the bonds." Ibn Kathir: "This is referring to the prisoners of war whom you have captured." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the point of law: once war has broken the might and power of the enemy and done away with their pomp and glory, they are to be *arrested rather than killed*.

**فَإِمَّا مَنَّۢا بَعْدُ وَإِمَّا فِدَآءً** — "then either an act of grace afterwards, or ransom." Ibn Kathir: after the war ends, there is a choice regarding the captives — "You may either act graciously toward them by setting them free without charge, or free them for a ransom that you require from them." Maʿārif notes that ransom can take more than one form: exchanging Muslim prisoners of war for non-Muslim prisoners, or release against a payment.

## Badr in the background

Ibn Kathir says it appears this ayah was revealed after the battle of Badr. At Badr, Allah had reproached the believers for sparing many of the enemy's soldiers and holding too many captives in order to take ransom from them, saying:

> "It is not for a Prophet to have captives of war until he had made a great slaughter in the land. You desire the commodities of this world, but Allah desires for you the Hereafter... Were it not for a prior decree from Allah, a severe torment would have touched you for what you took." (8:67–68)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have said that a grave punishment of Allah for that action was very close, and had it been meted out, no one would have been spared except ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh — because those two Companions alone had disagreed with the idea of accepting payment for releasing the prisoners.

## The scholars on ransom and captives

**The abrogation view.** Most of the Companions and jurists held that this ayah of Sūrah Muḥammad abrogated the ruling in Sūrah al-Anfāl. Tafsīr Mazharī records this as the position of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and the majority of the Companions and jurists; among the jurists Thawrī, Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Isḥāq also held it. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the sequence: at Badr the Muslims were few, so releasing prisoners — for ransom or as a gesture of grace — was forbidden; once Islam and the Muslims went on to achieve total ascendancy, Allah abrogated the earlier ruling and revealed this ayah permitting both. Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh cites this in Tafsīr Mazharī as the authentic and preferred view, since the Prophet ﷺ himself acted on it and the Righteous Caliphs after him did the same. The chronology fits: al-Anfāl came down at Badr in year 2 of the Hijrah, while the prisoners the Prophet ﷺ released without ransom at Ḥudaybiyah in year 6 were released in accordance with this ayah.

Maʿārif cites that practice from the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, on the authority of Anas: about eighty Makkans climbed down from Mount Tanʿīm intending a sudden attack on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslim camp. All were captured — and he ﷺ set them free without any compensation, lest it become the cause of war on that critical occasion. Concerning this, Allah revealed: "It is He who held their hands back from you, and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah, after giving you victory over them." (48:24)

**The opposite reading.** According to one version, a popular view of Imām Abū Ḥanīfah is that releasing prisoners of war, with or without ransom, is not lawful — and on that basis Ḥanafī scholars treated this ayah as abrogated by al-Anfāl. Maʿārif responds that Tafsīr Mazharī settled the chronology the other way: al-Anfāl came first, Sūrah Muḥammad later, so the later text repeals the earlier. It adds that Ibn al-Humām in *Fatḥ al-Qadīr* inclined to the majority view, noting that while Qudūrī and Hidāyah report Abū Ḥanīfah as disallowing release against ransom, another version of his view in *as-Siyar al-Kabīr* permits it in conformity with the majority — and that this latter is more likely his preferred position, as Imām Ṭaḥāwī also recorded in his *Maʿānī al-Āthār*.

**The view that nothing is abrogated.** Maʿārif sums up that, according to the majority of the Companions and jurists, neither of these two verses is abrogated: their wordings read not as abrogator and abrogated but as two rulings for two different situations, and the leader of the Muslims may adopt whichever option the conditions and needs of the Muslims require. Qurṭubī reached the same result from the practice of the Prophet ﷺ and the Righteous Caliphs. Both texts, he concludes, are *muḥkam* — operative and clear — and when the disbelievers come into Muslim control the leader has four options: he may kill them; he may hold them in bondage; he may release them for ransom or in exchange for Muslim prisoners; or he may release them outright. Maʿārif notes this as the view of the scholars of Madinah, Imām Shāfiʿī and Abū ʿUbayd, and that Ṭaḥāwī cites it from Abū Ḥanīfah too. On killing and bondage there is consensus in the Ummah as to permissibility; on release, with or without ransom, there is some difference, though the majority of jurists hold it lawful as well.

**Why the ayah mentions only release.** If killing and bondage are permitted, why name only grace and ransom? Imām Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī answers this in his Tafsīr Kabīr: the options named here are those that apply where the others are not open — it is not permissible to enslave Arab prisoners of war, nor is it lawful to kill the crippled — and besides, the question of killing had already been dealt with elaborately earlier. Maʿārif adds a second answer: the permissibility of killing and enslaving was common knowledge; what was new — and what had been forbidden at Badr — was release. Maʿārif reinforces this by pointing out that prisoners were held in bondage by the Prophet ﷺ and by the Companions after him in many battles that came *after* these ayat were revealed, and that had the permission been withdrawn, its prohibition would have been stated somewhere in the Qur'an or in a Hadith.

**On bondage.** Maʿārif stresses that this option is bare permissibility — not obligatory, not even commendable — and that the collective teachings of the Qur'an and Ḥadīth lead us to believe that emancipation is the more meritorious course, which is why freeing a slave is the first command prescribed as expiation for violating a fast, for murder, for ẓihār and for violated oaths and vows. It quotes the Prophet ﷺ: "Your slaves are your brothers, and Allah has put them under your control. So whoever has a brother under his command should feed him of what he eats, and dress him of what he wears. Do not overburden them to do things beyond their capacity, and if you do so, then help them" (recorded, as Maʿārif names it, by Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and others). ʿAlī reported that the last words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before he left this world were: "Take care of prayer; take care of prayer. Keep your duty to Allah regarding those under your command." And Maʿārif adds a ruling for our own time: where states have entered into covenants barring either side from enslaving the other's prisoners, that clause is binding while the agreement stands.

## "Until the war lays down its burden"

**حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا** — "until the war lays down its burden." Mujāhid said this means: until ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) descends. Ibn Kathir remarks that Mujāhid seems to have derived this from the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "There will always be a group of my Ummah victorious upon the truth, until the last of them fight against the Dajjāl."

Ibn Kathir then relates a scene that gives the phrase its weight. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Salamah ibn Nufayl, that he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "I have let my horse go, and thrown down my weapon, for the war has ended. There is no more fighting." The Prophet ﷺ answered him: "Now the time of fighting has come. There will always be a group of my Ummah dominant over others... until Allah's command comes to pass while they are in that state. Verily, the centre of the believers' abode is Ash-Shām. And goodness is tied around the horses' foreheads till the Day of Resurrection." An-Nasāʾī also recorded this narration.

## Why Allah did not simply take vengeance Himself

**ذَٰلِكَ وَلَوْ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ لَٱنتَصَرَ مِنْهُمْ** — "That; and had Allah willed, He could have taken vengeance upon them." Ibn Kathir: had He so willed, He could have taken immediate vengeance against the disbelievers with a chastisement or exemplary punishment directly from Him. **وَلَٰكِن لِّيَبْلُوَاْ بَعْضَكُم بِبَعْضٍ** — "but so that He may test some of you by means of others." Ibn Kathir: He has ordered jihād and fighting against the enemies in order to try you and test your affairs. He cites 3:142 — "Or did you think that you would enter Paradise before Allah had made evident those of you who fight in His cause and made evident those who are steadfast?" — and 9:14–15, where Allah says He will punish them by your hands, disgrace them, grant you victory over them, and satisfy the breasts of a believing people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out: the legalising of armed struggle in Allah's cause is itself a blessing, because it *replaces* the celestial punishments that fell on earlier nations. Previous peoples were punished with calamities from heaven and earth for their disbelief, idolatry and rebellion; this Ummah has been spared destruction by such general calamities, because the Prophet ﷺ is a mercy to mankind, and jihād according to the Sharīʿah was instituted in their place. In a general calamity an entire nation is decimated, men, women and children alike, whereas under the rules of war women and children are safe and secure, and among the men only those who commit aggression and violence against those who protect the religion of Allah face the believers — and even of those, not all are killed, since many come to embrace Islam or live as subjects of an Islamic state. The second wisdom, Maʿārif notes, is that both sides are tested: which side is willing to sacrifice life and wealth at Allah's command, and which side goes on stubbornly rejecting the truth after seeing its crystal-clear evidence.

## The martyrs: nothing is lost

**وَٱلَّذِينَ قُتِلُواْ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَلَن يُضِلَّ أَعْمَٰلَهُمْ** — "And those who are killed in the way of Allah, He will never let their deeds be lost." Ibn Kathir notes that since it is customary during wars that many of the believers die, Allah says this. He would not let their good deeds go to waste, says Ibn Kathir, but would rather multiply and increase them, and some of them will continue being rewarded for their good deeds for the entire length of their stay in al-Barzakh — the interval between death and the Resurrection.

Maʿārif points out the sharp contrast with the opening of the sūrah: there, the deeds of those who persist in disbelief and obstruct others from Islam are rendered void — charity, alms, donations, public welfare, all of it — because faith is the necessary condition for a good work to be rewarded in the next world. Those who sacrificed their lives in Allah's cause will never have their works imprinted with ruin; and even if they committed sins, Maʿārif says, those sins will not have a negative impact on their good actions — in fact their good deeds will often serve as an expiation for their sins.

Imām Aḥmad recorded in his Musnad, on the authority of Kathīr ibn Murrah from Qays al-Judhāmī, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "As the first drop of his blood gushes forth, a martyr is granted six merits: all of his sins are forgiven, he is shown his place in Paradise, he is married to wide-eyed ḥūrīs, he is secured from the great fear on the Day of Judgement and from the torment of the grave, and he is adorned with the adornments of īmān." Ibn Kathir notes that Aḥmad was alone in recording this hadith. And Abū al-Dardāʾ reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A martyr is allowed to intercede for seventy members of his household" — recorded by Abū Dāwūd.

## Ayah 5: guided, and set right

**سَيَهْدِيهِمْ** — "He will guide them." Ibn Kathir: He will guide them to Jannah, as in 10:9, "Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous good deeds, their Lord will guide them because of their faith: beneath them rivers will flow in the Gardens of Pleasure." Maʿārif reads this guidance as Allah causing them, through the Holy Prophet ﷺ, to reach their desired destination, which is Paradise — and cites the words the people of Paradise will say on entering it: "All praise to Allah who has led us unto this" (7:43).

**وَيُصْلِحُ بَالَهُمْ** — "and He will set right their state." Ibn Kathir glosses this as their situation and affairs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it out: "state of affairs" includes the conditions of both worlds. Even a Muslim who did not attain the glorious privilege of a martyr in this world will receive the reward of a martyr; in the Hereafter he will be spared the torment of the grave and the anxiety of the Resurrection; and if he violated the rights of other people, Allah will take upon Himself the responsibility of vindicating him and clearing him of all blame.

## Ayah 6: a Paradise they already know

**وَيُدْخِلُهُمُ ٱلْجَنَّةَ عَرَّفَهَا لَهُمْ** — "and He will admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them." Ibn Kathir: He has acquainted them with Paradise and guided them to it. Mujāhid said: "The people of Paradise will be guided to their houses and dwellings and whatever sections Allah has ordained for them in it. They will not make mistakes in this, nor will they ask anyone for directions to their dwellings — as if they had dwelt in it from the time they were first created."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the third bounty and makes the human point: He will not only admit them to Paradise but identify for them the gardens of bliss and make them familiar with its bounties, so that it would seem to them they had been living there since eternity. Without such an acquaintance, Maʿārif says, Paradise would have seemed a strange world. The gift is not only entry, but belonging.

Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "After the believers securely pass the Fire, they will be held back upon a bridge between Paradise and the Fire. There, they will have any acts of injustice that they committed against one another in the life of this world rectified. After they are completely purified and cleansed, they will be admitted into Paradise. By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, each one of them will find his way to his dwelling in Paradise better than he found his way to his dwelling in the worldly life." And Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Him who sent me with the religion of Truth! As you are closely familiar with your wives and homes in this world, so you will know your abode and your wives of Paradise — rather even better." Maʿārif adds that some reports mention an angel appointed for every single inhabitant of Paradise to introduce them to their abode — and closes, as the scholars do, with *Allāhu aʿlam*, Allah knows best.

## What the passage asks of us

Read whole, these ayat teach restraint as much as resolve. Ayah 4 is fierce while the enemy is still fighting and immediately merciful once he is not: the same verse that says strike the necks says bind them, then release them freely or for ransom. Nor are the rules the individual fighter's to improvise: as Qurṭubī and Maʿārif both frame it, the decision about captives belongs to the leader of the Muslims, weighed against the best interest of the Muslims.

And ayat 5–6 answer the fear underneath any sacrifice: that it might be for nothing. Maʿārif's reading is generous — the promise of having one's state set right reaches beyond the battlefield to the ordinary believer, who may receive the martyr's reward without the martyr's death. Whatever you spend for Allah is not dropped, not mislaid, not forgotten. Allah does not merely accept it; He multiplies it, keeps rewarding it through the long stay in al-Barzakh, takes upon Himself the claims others hold against you, and then brings you into a home you already recognise.

passages.title: If you support Allah, He will support you
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form a single unit: a contract offered, and the exact reverse of that contract shown in those who refused it. Ayah 7 puts the offer in one breath — support Allah, and He supports you and steadies your feet. Ayat 8 and 9 hold up the mirror image: instead of firm footing, misery; instead of deeds preserved, deeds made vain — and ayah 9 names the cause, which turns out to lie in the heart.

## A word on what "supporting Allah" can possibly mean

A reader stops at once on the wording: Allah is in need of nothing, so what could it mean for us to *support* Him? Ibn Kathir has already answered this a few lines earlier in the same passage. On Allah's words *had Allah so willed, He could have taken vengeance against them*, he explains that had He so willed, He could have taken immediate vengeance against the disbelievers with a chastisement or exemplary punishment directly from Him. No human effort was ever required. Ibn Kathir then comments on the continuation, *but He lets you struggle so as to test with one another*: Allah "has ordered Jihad and fighting against the enemies in order to try you and test your affairs."

So the "support" of ayah 7 is not Allah making up a shortfall. It is a trial He wisely ordained, in which His servants are shown for what they are. Ibn Kathir brings in two other places where Allah gives the same wisdom: *Or did you think that you would enter the Paradise before Allah had made evident those of you who fight in His cause and made evident those who are steadfast?* (3:142), and *Fight them; Allah will then punish them by your hands, disgrace them, grant you victory over them...* (9:14–15). Notice the words of that second ayah as Ibn Kathir quotes it — Allah punishes them *by your hands*. The power is His; the hands are ours. That is the logic of "supporting Allah" in a single phrase.

## Ayah 7: "If you support Allah, He will support you"

*O you who believe! If you support (the cause of) Allah, He will support you and make your foothold firm.*

The Arabic is spare and evenly balanced: *in tanṣurū Allāha yanṣurkum* — you support, He supports. The same verb, *naṣara* (to support, to aid, to come to someone's help), is used on both sides of the sentence. Nothing sits between the two halves.

Ibn Kathir reads this alongside *Indeed, Allah will surely support those who support Him (His cause)* (22:40), and then states the principle underneath both: **"the reward is comparable to the type of deed that is performed."** That is worth sitting with. Allah's response here is not merely generous — it is *matched*. It returns in the same currency it was paid in. Give support, and support is what comes back to you. The principle quietly warns as much as it promises: a person who gives Allah's cause nothing should not expect the kind of help he never offered.

Then the second half: *wa yuthabbit aqdāmakum* — **"and make your foothold firm."** Of everything Allah could have named as the reward for supporting His cause, He names *steadiness*. Ibn Kathir's own summary heading over this stretch of tafsir is simply: "Support Allah's Cause, He will then support You." And in his comment on the next ayah he identifies whose feet these are — "the believers who support the cause of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ." Supporting Allah, in his phrasing, is supporting what He revealed and the Messenger ﷺ He sent with it.

## Ayah 8: the photographic negative

*But as for those who disbelieve — misery awaits them, and Allah will make their deeds vain.*

Ibn Kathir points out the structure explicitly, and it is the key to the whole passage: **"This misery is the opposite of making firm the footholds of the believers who support the cause of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ."** Set ayah 7 and ayah 8 side by side and the mirror is exact. One party is planted; the other is in the state the Arabic calls *taʿs* — rendered here as misery. One party is promised firmness; the other's deeds are made vain, which Ibn Kathir glosses as: **"He will nullify them and make them fruitless."**

There is also an echo worth hearing between this ayah and what Allah said earlier in the same passage about those killed in His way — *fa-lan yuḍilla aʿmālahum*, "He will never let their deeds be lost." Here, of the disbelievers, He says *wa aḍalla aʿmālahum*, "and He will make their deeds vain." The same verb, negated for the one who gave himself to Allah's cause, and affirmed against the one who refused it. Two lives full of effort; only one of them arrives anywhere.

**The servant of the dinar.** At exactly this point Ibn Kathir cites a saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which he introduces as having been confirmed. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Misery awaits the servant of the Dinar; misery awaits the servant of the Dirham; misery awaits the servant of velvet. Misery awaits him, and degeneracy; and if he is pricked by a thorn, may he not find anyone to pull it for him."* Ibn Kathir explains that last phrase: **"This means may Allah not cure him."** (The bundle of tafsir before us does not name the collection this hadith was recorded in, so I do not name one either.)

Two things stand out. First, the hadith opens with the very word Allah uses in ayah 8 — the misery pronounced over those who rejected the revelation is pronounced by the Prophet ﷺ over a man who has made himself a *servant*, an ʿabd, of a coin or a piece of fine cloth. Second, look at how small the injury in the picture is: not catastrophe, but a thorn — and no relief for it. Read against the promise of ayah 7, the question this passage puts to a believer is not only whether he has religion, but what he is actually resting his weight on.

## Ayah 9: the reason, and it lies in the heart

*That is because they hate that which Allah has sent down; so He has made their deeds fruitless.*

Ayah 9 is the diagnosis behind the ruin of ayah 8. Ibn Kathir's gloss is deliberately plain: it means **"they did not want or like what Allah revealed."** Not that they never heard it, or weighed it and found the case wanting. They found it distasteful. The verdict of ayah 8 is therefore not arbitrary — it is the outward shape of an inward refusal, and Allah states the cause so that no one imagines the loss came out of nowhere.

The closing verb, *fa-aḥbaṭa aʿmālahum*, Ibn Kathir renders simply as: **"so He made their deeds fruitless."** Deeds were done — real effort, real expense, perhaps things that looked fine from the outside. But the passage places the whole weight on what a life is turned toward. Ayah 8 said their deeds are made vain; ayah 9 says they are made fruitless, and names the reason. They lead nowhere, and they weigh nothing.

## Living it

**Stop asking whether Allah needs you.** Ibn Kathir settles that: had Allah so willed, He could have taken immediate vengeance on the disbelievers directly from Him. The struggle He commanded was ordained, in Ibn Kathir's words, "in order to try you and test your affairs." Every chance to serve His religion is part of that wisdom, not a gap in His arrangement.

**Expect the return to match the offering.** Ibn Kathir's rule — the reward is comparable to the type of deed performed — means ayah 7 is not a lottery. Support given to Allah's cause with your time, wealth, tongue and body is met with support; and the particular form it takes is *steadiness*, which is exactly what a person under pressure needs and cannot manufacture for himself.

**Watch what you are actually standing on.** The words of the Prophet ﷺ about the servant of the dinar, the dirham and velvet turn ayah 8 from a description of other people into a mirror. Whatever a person has quietly made his master cannot make his foothold firm.

**Guard the heart's attitude to revelation.** Ayah 9 traces total ruin back to one thing: disliking what Allah sent down. The believer's protection is the opposite posture — receiving what Allah revealed willingly, especially the parts of it that cut against what he wants.

passages.title: The ruins of the past and the two destinies
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take the argument of the surah out of the battlefield and set it against the whole sweep of history: the ruined towns of earlier peoples are placed in front of the deniers as evidence, and then the reason behind every such ending is named — Allah stands as Protector of the believers, and the disbelievers have no protector at all. What holds the passage together is that single hinge word in ayah 11, **mawlā**. Ayah 10 shows what happens to a people with no protector; ayah 12 shows where each of the two parties finally comes to rest.

## Ayah 10 — "Have they not travelled through the land?"

Ibn Kathir identifies the ones being questioned: **those who associate partners with Allah and who deny His Messenger ﷺ**. The question is not an invitation to sightseeing. Allah asks them to do two things — to *travel* and then to *look* (`fa-yanẓurū`), because the first without the second changes nothing. Their eyes had passed over the wreckage of earlier peoples without ever once reading it.

What they are asked to look at is the **ʿāqibah** — the "end", how the story of those before them finished. A nation is not judged by its opening chapters, its wealth or its walls, but by how the account closed.

**"Allah destroyed them completely"** — `dammara Allāhu ʿalayhim`. Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that **Allah punished them because of their denial and disbelief, and saved the believers from among them**. This is easy to skim past, but it is the whole point. The destruction was not a blind catastrophe that swallowed everyone standing in one place. It was a judgement that sorted people: one group destroyed for rejection, another group rescued. That rescue is exactly why ayah 11 can say Allah is the *mawlā* of the believers — history has already demonstrated it.

**"And for the disbelievers are the likes thereof"** (`wa lil-kāfirīna amthāluhā`). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a small grammatical detail with a sharp edge: the definite article **alif-lām** in `al-kāfirīn` here points to *specific* disbelievers, and refers to **the disbelievers of Makkah**. The sentence is therefore not a general observation about unbelief in the abstract; it is a warning delivered to a named audience. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the purpose of the sentence: as the previous generations were punished for their iniquity, so will you meet a similar fate for your iniquitous behaviour — *do not be unconcerned*.

## Ayah 11 — The one word the passage turns on

**"That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector."**

Notice how the ayah opens: **"That is because…"** It is not a new subject. It is the reason standing behind ayah 10. Why were some destroyed and others saved? Not numbers, not fortifications, not fortune. Because one party had Allah as their *mawlā* and the other had no *mawlā* whatsoever.

**What "mawlā" means here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that `mawlā` is used in several different senses. One of its meanings is **"protector" or "supporter"** — and that is the sense in which it is used in this ayah. Another sense of the word is **"owner / master"**, and Maʿārif points to another passage where Allah says of people returned to Him: *"They will be returned to Allah, their Master, the Truth"* (10:30). In that phrase, Allah is called the `mawlā` **of the disbelievers too** — that is, their Master and Owner, because the mastership and ownership of Allah extends over all, the believers as well as the non-believers, without any exclusion.

So there is no contradiction between the two verses, and the distinction matters. In terms of **ownership**, no creature escapes Allah — the disbeliever is as much His as the believer. In terms of **protection and support**, the disbeliever has nothing and no one. He is owned but unaided. The believer, by contrast, has as his ally the One who owns everything.

## The day these words were shouted across a battlefield

Ibn Kathir attaches to this ayah one of the most striking scenes in the Prophet's ﷺ life — the aftermath of **Uḥud**.

Abu Sufyan Sakhr bin Harb, the commander of the idolaters at that time, inquired about the Prophet ﷺ, then about Abu Bakr, then about ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them. When he heard no response, he announced: **"Verily, those three have died!"**

ʿUmar then responded to him: **"You lie, O enemy of Allah! Allah has indeed saved those who will displease you. Indeed, those whom you mentioned are all alive!"**

Abu Sufyan then said: "Well, today makes up for the day of Badr, and the war has its ups and downs. And indeed, you are going to find mutilation in the bodies of your dead that I did not command, nor did I prohibit." Then he turned around chanting the name of their greatest idol: **"Glory to Hubal, glory to Hubal."**

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Aren't you going to respond to him?"* The Companions said: "What should we say, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said: **"Say: Allah is Most High and Most Glorious."**

Then Abu Sufyan said: "We have Al-ʿUzzā, and you have no ʿUzzā." Again the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Aren't you all going to respond to him?"* They said: "What should we say, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: **"Say: Allāhu mawlānā wa lā mawlā lakum — Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector."**

Sit with the timing of that. It is not said from a position of visible strength. It is said on a day of heavy loss, with the enemy standing over mutilated dead and counting the day as repayment for Badr, chanting the names of his idols. And the reply the Prophet ﷺ teaches is not a boast about tomorrow's revenge; it is a statement about *who each side actually has*. Their idol has a name and nothing behind it. The believers have Allah — and the outcome of a single afternoon does not touch that fact.

When ayah 11 says the same words back to us, it is telling the believer what to hold on to precisely on the days when the scoreboard looks wrong. (Ibn Kathir relates this exchange in his commentary without naming a collection at this point, so it is passed on here exactly as he transmits it.)

## Ayah 12 — The two destinies, deliberately unequal

**"Indeed Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow; while those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat — and the Fire is their abode."**

Look at how the two halves are built, because the imbalance is the message.

**The believers' half is entirely about the future.** "Allah *will admit*" — Ibn Kathir specifies: **on the Day of Resurrection**. Nothing is said here about their present comfort. And notice the condition is doubled: *believe* **and** *do righteous deeds*. Faith that never reaches the limbs is not what is being described. The entry itself is credited to Allah — *Allah* admits them; it is His act toward those to whom He is *mawlā*, not a wage they extracted from Him.

**The disbelievers' half is entirely about the present.** "They enjoy themselves and they eat" — an activity in progress, going on right now, going nowhere. Ibn Kathir's comment is unsparing: the disbelievers **enjoy their worldly life and eat in it like animals, munching and gnawing with greed. They have no concern other than that.**

That is the sting of the comparison to `al-anʿām`, grazing livestock. The ayah does not say they *are* cattle; it says they *eat as cattle eat*. An animal at a trough is not evil — it is simply operating without a horizon. It eats, is satisfied, eats again, and no part of it asks what any of it is for. A human being given revelation, given a Messenger, given the ruins of past nations to walk through, and who still lives with no question larger than the next appetite, has chosen the horizon of livestock while carrying the capacity for Paradise.

**And then the sentence lands: "the Fire is their abode."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: **on the Day of their Reckoning**. So the two clauses are not really parallel at all. The eating and the enjoying belong to this life; the Fire is what is waiting at the reckoning. One party is given a future; the other is given a present that runs out.

Ibn Kathir cites here what **has been confirmed in the Ṣaḥīḥ**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"A believer eats with one intestine, and a disbeliever eats with seven intestines."**

He brings it to illuminate exactly this contrast. Appetite is not merely a bodily fact; it tracks what a person is living for. The one whose sights are set beyond this world eats to keep going. The one for whom this world is the whole account has nothing to be filled by except more of it — and so is never filled.

## What the "Gardens beneath which rivers flow" hold

Ayah 12 promises Gardens with rivers running beneath them. Later in this same surah those rivers are described in detail, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting there, lists four kinds of favours and blessings of the next world: rivers of **pure water**, rivers of **milk whose taste does not change**, rivers of **wine which gives delight**, and rivers of **purified honey** — given to the righteous in plenty.

Its treatment is instructive. Each of these exists here in a degraded form. Worldly waters become polluted by mixing with earth, vegetation and other adulterating substances that make them stink. Milk, once secreted, soon starts to deteriorate. Worldly wine has a foul smell and a bitter taste, though those addicted to it no longer feel the bitterness, being accustomed to it. Honey, when extracted from the comb, needs to be clarified of wax, scum and other unwanted substances. The Paradise versions are these same realities with the corruption removed: water that will not go bad in taste, smell or colour; milk that will never be spoilt, eternally delicious; wine that gives endless delight to the drinker, which the Qur'an elsewhere describes as having no headache in it, nor will they be intoxicated by it (37:47); honey that is pure and clean and amply available — all of it flowing uninterrupted, without layers of dregs, scum or any other unpleasant-looking substance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that all four are used in their **primary senses**; there is no need to apply them unnecessarily in a figurative sense. But it adds the necessary caution: it is obvious that the bounties of Paradise cannot be compared to the things of this world. Their taste and quality will be unique and can only be experienced in the gardens of Paradise. The familiar names are a bridge for our imagination, not a ceiling on the reality.

## Where the argument is heading

Ibn Kathir reads these ayat as running straight on into what follows, where Allah asks how many a town **mightier than your town, which drove you out**, He has destroyed with none to help them — and "your town" here means **Makkah**. He calls this **a great threat and a severe warning to the people of Makkah**, because they rejected the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was the chief of the Messengers and the last of the Prophets. That is the direction ayat 10–12 have been pointing all along: the ruins are not a museum exhibit but an argument, and the argument has an addressee.

## Living it

**Read the ruins.** Ayah 10 makes history a form of evidence. Every collapsed power was once certain it was the exception. Travelling, reading, watching events unfold — all of it is wasted unless the second verb happens: *look*, and ask how the account closed.

**Know which mawlā you are claiming.** Ayah 11 permits no third option: Allah as Protector, or no protector at all. Everything else a person leans on — status, wealth, connections, a slogan shouted from a hilltop — is somebody's Hubal.

**Say it on the bad day.** The Prophet ﷺ taught those words after a defeat, not after a victory. That is when they are worth the most.

**Check the horizon of your appetites.** Ayah 12 does not condemn eating or enjoying; it condemns a life in which eating and enjoying are the entire agenda — "they have no concern other than that," as Ibn Kathir puts it. The believer's question is always: what lies beyond this? Keep that question alive and the same meal that lets one life shrink to a trough becomes fuel for something lasting.

**Do not envy the present tense.** The disbelievers in this ayah are visibly enjoying themselves — the Qur'an states it plainly rather than hiding it. It simply asks you to read the sentence to its end.

passages.title: Clear proof or blind desire, and where each ends
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take one question and drive it all the way to its end. Ayah 13 points to towns that were mightier than Makkah and were destroyed with no one to help them. Ayah 14 draws the line that decides everything: a person standing on clear evidence from his Lord, or a person whose evil deed has been made to look beautiful to him so that he follows his own cravings. Ayah 15 then shows where each of those two roads finishes — rivers that never spoil, or boiling water that severs the insides. Evidence or desire; garden or fire. That is the unit.

## "How many a town mightier than your town"

Ayah 13 is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, but every word of it is aimed at the people who drove him out. Ibn Kathir says plainly that "your town that has driven you out" means Makkah, and that the phrase means *its people* who expelled him from among them.

Ibn Kathir calls this ayah **a great threat and severe warning to the people of Makkah**, and his reasoning is worth following closely. Allah had destroyed earlier nations because they denied their Messengers. The Makkans rejected Allah's Messenger ﷺ — "the chief of the Messengers and the last of the Prophets." So what, Ibn Kathir asks, should they expect Allah would do to them in this worldly life and in the Hereafter? And he adds a sobering note: if the torment were lifted from some of them in this life through the blessing of the presence of the Messenger, the Prophet of Mercy, it was not cancelled — it was stored up for them in the next life. He brings as evidence Allah's words about an earlier people, *"Their torment will be doubled! They could not bear to hear (the preaching), and they used not to see (the truth)"* (11:20).

The argument of the ayah is an argument from strength. Makkah was formidable — but the ayah says there were towns **"mightier in power"** than it, and their might bought them nothing. The sentence ends with a phrase that leaves no exit: **"with none to help them."** No ally, no rescue, no one who stood up when Allah's decree came.

Just before this, Ibn Kathir is commenting on Allah's words that He **"is the Protector (*mawlā*) of those who believe, whereas the disbelievers have no protector,"** and there he recounts a scene that gives that word a face. After the battle of Uhud, Abu Sufyan Sakhr bin Harb, then commander of the idolaters, called out asking after the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them. Hearing no answer, he announced that all three were dead. 'Umar could not hold back: "You lie, O enemy of Allah! Allah has indeed saved those who will displease you. Indeed, those whom you mentioned are all alive!" Abu Sufyan answered that the day made up for Badr, that war has its ups and downs, and admitted that mutilation would be found among the believers’ dead — something he neither ordered nor forbade. Then he turned away chanting, "Glory to Hubal, glory to Hubal," naming their greatest idol. The Prophet ﷺ said to his Companions, *"Aren't you going to respond to him?"* They asked what to say. He ﷺ said: **"Say: Allah is Most High and Most Glorious."** Abu Sufyan called again: "We have Al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza." Again the Prophet ﷺ asked, *"Aren't you all going to respond to him?"* and again they asked what to say. He ﷺ said: **"Say: Allah is our Protector (*mawlānā*), and you have no protector."**

Hold that answer beside ayah 13. The ruined towns had more power than Makkah — and, when the decree came, no helper at all.

## The Prophet ﷺ looking back at Makkah

Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Abi Hatim, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when Allah's Messenger ﷺ left Makkah at the Hijrah (the migration to Madinah) and reached the cave and hid inside it, he looked back toward the city and said:

> "You are the most beloved to Allah among Allah's lands, and you are also the most beloved to me among Allah's lands. Were it not that the idolaters have driven me out from you, I would never have left you."

Ibn 'Abbas then said: "The worst of enemies is he who transgresses against Allah in His own sacred place, who kills a person who is not trying to kill him, or who kills because of Jahiliyyah vengeance" — that is, the blood-feuds of the age of ignorance before Islam, in which a killing was answered by another killing to satisfy tribal honour. And it was then, Ibn 'Abbas said, that Allah revealed to His Prophet ﷺ this very ayah — *"And how many a town mightier than your town that has driven you out have We destroyed, with none to help them!"*

Feel the shape of that moment before moving on. The Prophet ﷺ is hiding, saying goodbye to the most beloved place on earth to him — a place he is leaving only because he was pushed out. He does not curse it. He praises it, and grieves. And Allah's answer to that grief is not a promise of revenge but a statement of fact: towns stronger than that one did this sort of thing before, and they were destroyed, and no one helped them. The ayah comforts by re-sizing the enemy.

## The fork: evidence or desire (ayah 14)

Then comes the question the whole passage turns on. Ibn Kathir titles his comment on it: **"The Worshipper of the Truth and the Worshipper of Lust are not Equal."**

**"He who stands on clear evidence (*bayyinah*) from his Lord."** Ibn Kathir explains this as a person who is upon **clear vision and certainty** concerning Allah's commands and His religion — and he names two sources for that clarity together: the guidance and knowledge Allah has revealed in His Book, and **the pure nature upon which Allah has created him**. That pairing is the heart of it. Revelation from outside, and an unspoiled inner disposition inside, agreeing with each other. And note that it is *"from his Lord"* — the clarity is not self-generated. He did not think his way to it; it was given.

**"Like one for whom the evil of his deed has been made to seem beautiful."** The ayah does not tell us here who did the beautifying — it tells us the result. The man does not see his wrongdoing as wrongdoing. It has been made attractive to him, so that what should repel him now appeals to him. And the ayah pairs that with what follows from it: **"while they follow their own lusts."** Notice the direction of travel — desire is not being restrained by evidence; it is being served.

So the passage sets against each other not simply a good man and a bad man, but a man with **clear sight** and a man with **decoration**. Ibn Kathir says the answer to the question is simply that **they cannot be equal**, and he brings two parallel verses to show the Qur'an's own pattern of asking it: *"Can he who knows that what has been revealed unto you from your Lord is the truth be like him who is blind?"* (13:19), and *"Not equal are the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise. The People of Paradise will be the successful ones."* (59:20). In the first, the contrast is sight against blindness — which is exactly the difference between clear evidence and cosmetics.

## Where each road ends (ayah 15)

Ayah 15 answers the question of ayah 14 not with an argument but with two images.

**"The description (*mathal*) of the Paradise promised to those who have taqwa"** — taqwa being that mindfulness of Allah which keeps a guard between a person and Allah's displeasure. 'Ikrimah said of the word *mathal* here simply: **"This means its description."** That is an important note. The ayah is not offering a poetic figure of speech; it is telling us what the place is like. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about the four rivers: they are used **in their primary senses**, and there is no need to apply them unnecessarily in a figurative sense. At the same time — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here — the bounties of Paradise cannot be compared to the things of this world. Their taste and quality are unique and can only be experienced there. So: real water, real milk, real wine, real honey — and yet not comparable to anything you have tasted.

Read the four rivers as four corrections of the flaws we know:

**Water that is not *āsin*.** On this word the early authorities are reported slightly differently. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Al-Hasan and Qatadah said it means **"it does not change."** Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and 'Ata' Al-Khurasani said it means **"it is not foul-smelling."** Ibn Kathir adds the linguistic basis: the Arabs say water is *asin* when its scent changes. The two readings are one reality seen from two sides — standing water in this world goes off, and you smell it before you taste it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture: worldly waters are polluted by earth, vegetation and other adulterating substances that make them stink; the river of Paradise will not go bad in taste, smell or colour, and will flow uninterruptedly, without dregs or scum.

**Milk whose taste never changes.** Ibn Kathir describes it as milk of the utmost whiteness, sweetness and richness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes what makes worldly milk what it is: it is secreted by the mammary glands of female mammals, and soon it starts to deteriorate. In Paradise it will flow in rivers and will never be spoilt; its taste will be eternally delicious. Ibn Kathir mentions a hadith attributed to the Prophet ﷺ — he does not name a collection for it — that *their milk did not come out of the udders of cattle*.

**Wine delightful to those who drink it.** Ibn Kathir says the wine of Paradise does not have a bad taste or foul smell as in this worldly life; it is good in its appearance, taste, smell **and effect** — and he cites Allah's own words: *"it has no bad effects, nor does it cause intoxication"* (37:47), *"From which they will have no headache, nor will they be intoxicated"* (56:19), *"white, delicious to the drinkers"* (37:46). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a shrewd observation about worldly wine: it has a foul smell and a bitter taste, though those addicted to it do not feel its bitterness, being accustomed to it — which is exactly the condition ayah 14 described, a thing that no longer looks or tastes like what it is. Ibn Kathir also mentions a hadith attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, again without naming a collection, that *their wine was not pressed under men's feet*.

**Refined honey.** Ibn Kathir: honey of the utmost purity, with pleasant colour, taste and smell. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces what worldly honey has to pass through — nectar drawn from flowers by bees, carried in their honey-sacs, changed, stored in the cells of the comb, ripened by evaporation, then extracted and clarified of wax, scum and other unwanted substances. The honey of Paradise will be pure and clean and amply available, flowing as rivers without dregs or scum. And Ibn Kathir mentions a hadith attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, again with no collection named, that *their honey did not come out of the bellies of bees*.

Do you see the single thread running through all four? Everything delicious in this world reaches us through a process of change, decay or dependency — it comes out of a body, it goes off, it must be filtered. The rivers of Paradise have the pleasure without the process.

**Where the rivers come from.** Ibn Kathir records that **Imam Ahmad** narrated from Hakim bin Mu'awiyah, from his father, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: *"Verily, there is in Paradise a lake of milk, a lake of water, a lake of honey, and a lake of wine. The rivers then gush out of them."* **At-Tirmidhi** reported this narration in his section on the Description of Paradise and said, **"Hasan Sahih."** And it is recorded **in the Sahih** that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: *"When you ask Allah, ask Him for Al-Firdaws, because it is the central and highest part of the Paradise, and from it gush the rivers of the Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful."*

That last hadith turns the description into an instruction. Do not merely admire these rivers — ask for the place they flow from, and ask for the highest of it.

**"And therein for them are all kinds of fruits."** Ibn Kathir links this to *"They will call in it for every kind of fruit in peace and security"* (44:55) and *"In them will be every kind of fruits in pairs"* (55:52).

**"And forgiveness from their Lord."** Ibn Kathir's comment on this is short and weighty: it means **in addition to all of the above**. After rivers and fruits, the list closes with the thing none of it could be enjoyed without. The rivers are what they are given; forgiveness is why they are there at all. And note who the promise is for — those who have taqwa. The man of clear evidence in ayah 14 and the people of taqwa in ayah 15 are described in the same breath of the passage; standing on evidence from your Lord is not a posture, it is a way of living.

**The counter-image.** Then, without transition, the ayah asks: **"Can this be likened to those who abide eternally in the Fire?"** Ibn Kathir puts the question in full: can those whose position in Paradise has just been described be like those who will abide eternally in the Fire? They are not equal — nor are those who will be in the high ranks and those who will be in the lowest depths. And the drink of that place is set exactly opposite the four rivers: **"and are given to drink boiling water"** — Ibn Kathir says extremely hot, so hot that it is unbearable — **"that severs their intestines,"** cutting their insides, both bowels and intestines. Ibn Kathir adds the only response a believer can make: *We seek refuge in Allah from that.*

The parallel is deliberate. One group drinks and is delighted forever; the other drinks and is destroyed, again and again.

## Living it

**Test what has been made beautiful to you.** Ayah 14 does not describe a person who knows he is doing wrong and does it anyway. It describes someone whose evil deed has been made to look beautiful, so that it seems fine from the inside. The only defence the ayah names is its own opposite: *bayyinah* from your Lord — and Ibn Kathir names the two sources of that clarity together, the guidance and knowledge Allah revealed in His Book, and the pure nature Allah created you upon. If a habit of yours can only be defended by your own reasoning, and never by what Allah revealed, that is precisely the shape ayah 14 is warning about.

**Re-size what frightens you.** Ayah 13 was revealed, Ibn 'Abbas said, to a man in a cave, on the run, looking back at the city he loved most. Its comfort was not "they will pay" but "towns mightier than that one were destroyed, and there was none to help them."

**Ask for Firdaws.** The Prophet ﷺ did not leave us to admire Paradise from a distance; he told us what to name in our asking, and to aim at the highest part of it, from which the rivers gush and above which is the Throne of the Most Merciful.

passages.title: Hearing without heeding, as the Hour draws near
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat sit in a single gathering and then open out onto the end of the world. In ayah 16 we are shown people sitting in the Prophet's ﷺ own assembly, hearing revelation with their ears and carrying nothing away; ayah 17 turns to those who came to the same words and left richer than they arrived. Ayah 18 asks what such heedless listeners can possibly be waiting for, since the Hour is already sending its signs ahead of it. And ayah 19 turns from them to the Prophet ﷺ himself with the two things that answer everything the passage has exposed: hold fast to *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, and keep asking forgiveness. The thread running through all four is the difference between hearing and heeding — and the fact that time to close that gap is running out.

## The scene behind ayah 16

Ibn Kathir describes this as Allah exposing "the hypocrites' stupidity and limited understanding." They used to sit before Allah's Messenger ﷺ and listen to his words without understanding anything, and then, on leaving his presence, they would turn to the Companions — "those who have received knowledge" — and ask, **"What is it that he has said just now?"**

Sit with how strange that is. These are people physically closer to revelation than any of us will ever be. The Qur'an is being recited by the one it was revealed to; they are within arm's reach. And they walk out of the room empty. Ibn Kathir names two things about them together: "They did not understand what he said, nor did they care about it." Both failures are recorded side by side — the mind that did not take it in, and the heart that was not interested in taking it in.

**"Just now" — the word ānifan.** The Arabic *ānifan* means, as Ibn Kathir explains, "at this moment" — this instant, the words still hanging in the air. That single word is what makes the verse cut. They are not asking about a lesson from last month that had slipped their memory. They are asking about a sentence spoken seconds ago. The gap between hearing and retaining was as long as the walk to the door.

**"Some of them who listen to you."** Notice the verb: they *listen*. The passage does not accuse them of walking out, heckling, or refusing to attend. They were present, attentive in posture, part of the congregation. Their failure is invisible from the outside — which is precisely the nature of hypocrisy, and precisely why this is a warning to anyone who attends and does not absorb.

**Sealed hearts, followed desires.** Allah's verdict on them: *"Such are the men whose hearts Allah has sealed because they followed their lusts."* Ibn Kathir unpacks this as two distinct defects — it means "that they had neither sound understanding nor correct intentions." The intellect is not working and the will is not aimed right. And the ayah itself ties the sealing to what they did: it is stated as following upon their following of their desires. This is not an arbitrary lock placed on innocent hearts; the ayah names what they did.

## Ayah 17: the same words, the opposite result

Immediately Allah sets the mirror image beside them: *"And as for those who accept guidance, He increases them in guidance and bestows on them their taqwā."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is worth reading slowly: this means "that those who seek guidance, Allah facilitates it for them; He guides them to it, makes them firm on it, and gives them more of it." Four gifts stacked in one clause — He makes the path easy, He shows it, He steadies the feet on it, and then He adds to it. Guidance in this ayah is not a one-time handover; it is capital that compounds.

**"Their taqwā" — a gift, not an achievement.** *Taqwā* is that awareness of Allah which makes a person guard against whatever displeases Him. The ayah says Allah *gave* them their taqwā; Ibn Kathir renders the clause "He inspires them to their righteous guidance." So even the piety of the pious is a bestowal, not a self-made possession.

Placed against ayah 16, the pairing teaches something exact: two people can sit in the same room, under the same recitation, and one leaves with nothing while the other leaves with more than he came for. The difference is not access to the words.

## Ayah 18: what exactly are they waiting for?

*"Do they then await except that the Hour should come upon them suddenly?"* — Ibn Kathir: "meaning, while they are unaware of it." The question is a rebuke shaped as a question. A person who hears reminder after reminder and files none of it away is, whether he says so or not, betting on having time. The ayah calls that bet what it is.

**Ashrāṭ — the signs already delivered.** *"But already there have come some of its portents."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *ashrāṭ* here means "signs," and Ibn Kathir glosses it as "the signs of its approach." Both commentaries then make the same striking point: the first of those signs is the Prophet ﷺ himself. Ibn Kathir writes that "the Messenger's advent is one of the signs of the Hour, because he is the Finality of the Messengers. With him, Allah has completed the religion and established the evidence against all people in a way that was never done by a previous Prophet." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it the same way: the portents of the last Hour begin with the very advent of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ, because the end of prophethood is itself the sign that the Hour is near.

Al-Bukhari recorded from Sahl bin Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw Allah's Messenger ﷺ bring his index and middle fingers together and say: **"I have been sent before the Hour as these two (fingers)."** The gesture is the tafsir. There is a gap — the fingers are not one — but it is the gap between two fingers on a single hand.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the splitting of the moon is likewise counted among these early signs, citing the Qur'an's own words in 54:1, "The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split." Ibn Kathir gathers a cluster of verses saying the same thing in different registers: *"This is a warner of the warners of old. The approaching Day has drawn near"* (53:56–57); *"The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split"* (54:1); *"The command of Allah is coming, so do not be impatient for it"* (16:1); and, most pointedly for these particular listeners, *"The people's Day of Reckoning has approached while they turn away in heedlessness"* (21:1). That last verse is ayah 16 in miniature.

**Signs still to come.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records further portents foretold in authentic aḥādīth. Anas reports hearing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that among the signs of the last Hour are "the removal of knowledge, abundance of ignorance, the prevalence of fornication, the prevalence of wine-drinking, the small number of men and the large number of women so that fifty women will have one man to look after them" (Bukhari and Muslim); a version has "knowledge will dwindle and ignorance will be widespread."

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reports Allah's Messenger ﷺ as listing a long sequence: when spoils of war are taken as personal wealth, property given in trust is treated as spoil, zakāh is treated as a fine, learning is acquired for other than religious purpose, a man obeys his wife and is undutiful towards his mother, brings his friend near and drives his father far off, voices are raised in the mosques, the most wicked member of a tribe becomes its ruler and the most worthless member of a people its leader, a man is honoured through fear of the evil he may do, singing-girls and stringed instruments make their appearance, wines are drunk, and the last members of this community curse the earlier ones — then, he ﷺ said, look at that time for a violent wind, an earthquake, being swallowed up by the earth, metamorphosis, pelting rain, "and signs following one another like bits of a necklace falling one after the other when its string is cut" (Tirmidhi).

Read that list slowly and notice how many of its items are a right order turned upside down — trust treated as plunder, zakāh felt as a fine, learning pursued for something other than the religion, the mother set below the wife, the worst of a people at its head. And notice the closing image the hadith itself supplies: beads off a cut string do not fall at leisurely intervals; they fall one after the other.

**Why remembering then is too late.** *"And when it actually is on them, how can they benefit then by their reminder?"* Ibn Kathir: "how would remembering benefit the disbelievers when the Hour comes upon them?" He sets two verses beside it — *"On that Day will the human being remember, but what would that remembrance avail him then?"* (89:23), and *"They will say: 'Now we believe in it!' But how could they claim belief from such a far place?"* (34:52). The man of ayah 16, who could not hold a sentence for the length of a walk, will remember on that Day — and the remembering will not avail him. A reminder is only worth something while there is still time to act on it, which is exactly the argument this passage has been making since its first word.

## Ayah 19: know, then ask forgiveness

*"So know that lā ilāha illā Allāh, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women."*

**Why "know" and not "say"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: it is plain that every Muslim already has this knowledge — let alone the leader of the Prophets ﷺ, who has it most profoundly — so why is he commanded, through an imperative verb, to know it? Two answers are offered: either it means he is enjoined to be steadfast in his worship of Allah, or it means he must fulfil the demands of that knowledge.

That second answer opens onto a principle. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Qurtubi the incident of Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, may Allah have mercy on him, who, when asked about the significance of knowledge, replied by pointing to this very verse: "So know for sure that there is no god but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your fault." What the verse requires, he said, is that knowledge be acquired before action. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows the same pattern elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Know that the present life is but a sport and a diversion" (57:20) is followed by "Race to forgiveness from your Lord" (57:21); and in Sūrah al-Anfāl, "Know that your wealth and children are a trial" has its corresponding demand stated in Sūrah at-Taghābun, "so be fearful of Him" (64:14). First the knowledge is put in place, then the action it demands is called for. Here the knowledge is tawḥīd, and its first demand is istighfār.

Ibn Kathir touches the same joint from another angle: *lā ilāha illā Allāh* "is a declaration that there is no true deity except Allah. It is not something that is easy for him to command the people to have knowledge of. That is why Allah connected it with" the command to seek forgiveness.

**"Your sin" — how the scholars handle this.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the difficulty head on. The Prophet ﷺ is infallible and immune from sin, so the possibility that he would commit sins is unthinkable. What cannot be ruled out is a misjudgement in *ijtihād* — an exercise of considered judgement in a matter left to it. According to the sacred law such mistakes are not regarded as sins; in fact they are rewarded, though the prophets, peace be upon them, are told the correct position. Yet given the high status of the prophets, even these are sometimes referred to as *dhanb* (fault or sin) — as in Sūrah ʿAbasa, where the error of judgement referred to "was not really a sin," and a reward was in fact promised for it, but because it was not in conformity with that high status Allah expressed His dislike. It is *dhanb* in this sense, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, that the present verse means.

**What the Prophet ﷺ actually did with this command.** Ibn Kathir answers with the man's own words. Recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, he ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, forgive my sin, my ignorance, my immoderation in my affairs, and all that You know better about my faults than myself. O Allah, forgive for me my joking, my seriousness, my unintended error, and my deliberate mistakes — and I have done of all that." Also reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ, at the end of the prayer he ﷺ would say: "O Allah, forgive for me what I have previously done, what I may commit in future, what I have committed secretly, what I have committed openly, what I have done excessively, and all sins that You know better than me. You are my Lord. There is no true deity except You." And it is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that he ﷺ used to say: **"O people! Repent to your Lord! Verily, I ask Allah for forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times every day."**

More than seventy times a day — from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself. Istighfār, on this showing, is not merely the sinner's emergency exit; it is the ordinary breathing of the servant nearest to Allah.

**"And for the believing men and women."** The command widens without warning. Having been told to seek forgiveness for himself, he ﷺ is told to seek it for the believers, men and women named separately. The believer's istighfār is not a private ledger to be balanced alone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a report of Sayyidnā Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said to recite *lā ilāha illā Allāh* and istighfār frequently, because Iblis says: I got people involved in sins and destroyed them, but they destroyed me by reciting *illā Allāh*, so I got them involved instead in false and baseless thoughts and notions which they pursue as true, authentic and righteous — the common religious innovations (*bidʿah*), which they treat as righteous — and so they do not feel any need to repent for them. That is the stratagem the report names: a practice held to be righteousness is not brought to repentance, because the person sees nothing in it to repent of. And the two remedies commanded in ayah 19 are exactly the two the report says Iblis fears — the word of tawḥīd, and the habit of asking forgiveness.

**The closing clause.** *"And Allah knows well your moving about (mutaqallabakum) and your place of rest (mathwākum)."* Ibn Kathir: "He knows how you behave during the day, and where you settle at night," comparing "It is He Who takes your souls by night and knows all that you do by day" (6:60) and "there is no moving creature on earth but its provision is up to Allah, and He knows its dwelling place and its deposit — all is in a clear register" (11:6).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two words lexically. *Mutaqallab* means "turning around or turning over"; *mathwā* means "permanent resting place." The phrase is open to several interpretations, and the commentators have accordingly assigned different meanings to it — all of which, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds, are correct and sound, because human beings are confronted by two types of condition, the temporary and the permanent, and likewise stay in some places temporarily and in others permanently. In this verse *mutaqallab* describes the temporary and *mathwā* the permanent. The sum of it: Allah is fully aware of all conditions of a human being.

Read as the seal of this passage, that clause answers the people of ayah 16 precisely. They could leave the gathering and behave as though the words had never been spoken. But the One who spoke them knows the movement out of the door — and the place they finally come to rest.

## Living it

- **Attendance is not reception.** Ayah 16 indicts people who were physically present at the best gathering on earth. Ask, after any khutbah or class: what did he say just now — and can I answer?
- **Guard the intention as much as the intellect.** Ibn Kathir names both defects together: no sound understanding, no correct intentions — and the ayah states the sealing of their hearts alongside their following of their desires.
- **Ask for guidance as an ongoing supply.** Ayah 17 promises increase to those who seek it, and even taqwā is something Allah bestows — so ask Him for it rather than treating it as your own achievement.
- **Treat the signs as a clock, not a spectacle.** The point of the *ashrāṭ* in ayah 18 is not curiosity about dates; it is that reminder is only useful while there is still time to act on it.
- **Build the two habits of ayah 19.** Renew the knowledge of *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, and make istighfār constant — for yourself, and for the believing men and women — following the one who did it more than seventy times a day.
