passages.title: Hypocrites' dread when fighting is ordained
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat expose what happens inside a community when a long-awaited command finally arrives. The believers had been asking for a sūrah that would legislate fighting; when it came, the people with sickness in their hearts stared at the Prophet ﷺ like men already dying. Ayah 20 sets up the contrast, ayah 21 names what would have served them better, ayah 22 asks what they would really do with themselves if they walked away, and ayah 23 pronounces the verdict on such people. One question runs through all four: what does a heart do when obedience stops being talk and becomes cost?

## The command they asked for

Ibn Kathir explains that the believers were *hoping* Jihad would be legislated — they were the ones saying, "Why is not a sūrah sent down for us?" — meaning a sūrah containing the order to fight. But when Allah ordained it, many of the people turned back.

He draws the parallel with an earlier passage that describes exactly the same reversal:

> "Have you not seen those who were told: 'Restrain your hands (from fighting), establish the Salah, and give Zakah.' But then when fighting was ordained for them, you find a party of them fearing the people as they fear Allah or more. They said: 'Our Lord! Why have You decreed fighting upon us? If only You have postponed us for a short period.' Say: 'The enjoyment of this world is little. The Hereafter is far better for him who had Taqwa of Allah, and you will not be dealt with unjustly, even as much as a thin thread inside a date's pit.'" (4:77)

Reading the two side by side is the fastest way into our passage. The same mouths that asked for the command asked to be excused from it. The distance between wanting a duty and carrying it is where hypocrisy becomes visible.

## Why "a decisive sūrah"

The ayah does not simply say "a sūrah"; it says **sūrah muḥkamah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *muḥkamah* lexically means "firm" — and in that lexical sense every sūrah of the Qur'an is *muḥkam*. But here the word carries its technical legal sense: in the language of the sacred law, *muḥkam* is used as the opposite of *mansūkh*, "abrogated." A *muḥkam* ruling is one that is in force, still operative, not superseded.

That single adjective explains the believers' eagerness. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, their longing for a new sūrah makes sense precisely because they wanted one that would embody an operative divine commandment that is not abrogated — something binding they could act on. Quoting Qurtubi, it reports that Qatādah said all sūrahs containing the injunctions of Jihād and Qitāl are operative and not abrogated; and since the main objective of this sūrah is to enjoin fighting and to persuade people to carry out the injunction, the description *sūrah muḥkamah* points precisely to that injunction.

So the believers were not asking for more recitation. They were asking to be given something firm to obey.

## The look of one about to faint

Then comes the image that gives the passage its charge: when the decisive sūrah was sent down mentioning fighting, "you can see those in whose hearts is disease looking at you with the look of one who is about to faint for fear of death."

Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and exact — this is because of "their fear, terror, and cowardice concerning meeting the enemies." Notice what the ayah photographs: not their words, but their *eyes*. The tongue can be managed; a glazed, rolling stare cannot. And the Prophet ﷺ is addressed directly — *you can see them* — so that what the heart hides is precisely what the face hands over.

## *Fa-awlā lahum* — two ways the scholars read it

The end of ayah 20, **fa-awlā lahum**, has been read in two ways, and both are represented in our sources.

Ibn Kathir treats it as encouragement and a missed good: it *would have been better for them*, and what would have been better is named immediately in ayah 21 — "obedience and good words," meaning, in his words, that it would have been better for them to listen and obey in that present situation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the other reading, from Aṣmaʿī by way of Qurtubi: the Arabic phrase means that **the causes of destruction have approached or drawn near to them** — destruction is very close to them. On this reading the phrase is a threat rather than an invitation.

Read together, the two put the same moment in view from opposite sides. Obedience was there for the taking; refusing it brings ruin near. The verse hangs between a door and a cliff.

## Obedience, honest speech, and the moment it gets real

Three short movements make up ayah 21, and Ibn Kathir walks through them.

**"Obedience and good words"** — the thing that would have been better for them: to listen and obey, right then, in that present situation, without haggling.

**"When the matter is resolved"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as *when the situation becomes serious and the time of fighting truly arrives*. This is the pivot of the whole passage. Talk is cheap in the planning stage; the matter becoming firm is what sorts people.

**"If they had been true to Allah"** — and here is the heart of it. Ibn Kathir glosses being true to Allah as **making their intentions sincerely for Him**. Truthfulness with Allah, on this reading, is not primarily about accurate speech; it is about an intention that matches the claim. Had they meant it, "it would have been better for them" — better for *them*. The loss in refusing was entirely their own.

## Turning away — and what it turns into

Having named what they refused, ayah 22 turns on them with a question: "So would you perhaps, if you turned away, spread corruption on earth, and sever your ties of kinship?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the verb **tawallā** carries two senses in Arabic: *iʿrāḍ*, turning away, and also being placed in authority over people. Both have been adopted by commentators.

**First reading — turning away.** Some commentators take it this way, and Abū Ḥayyān in *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* prefers it. The meaning then: if you turned away from Jihad and the other injunctions of the Sharīʿah, you would return to the ancient system of ignorance which Islam abolished. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out what that order looked like — in the days of *jāhiliyyah* they practised injustice, they cut each other's throats, one tribe attacked another, there was carnage and massacre, and they buried their daughters alive with their own hands. Islam abolished and wiped out these practices. Against those crimes, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, Islam enjoined Jihad, which apparently seems to be bloodshed but is in reality analogous to amputating a diseased limb of a body so that the rest of the body may remain healthy; Jihad establishes justice and equity and maintains the ties of kinship and relationship. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way: turning away from Jihad and withdrawing from it means going back to the old practices of the time of ignorance — shedding blood and severing kinship ties.

**Second reading — being given authority.** Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, Qurtubi and others take *tawallī* here as being placed in authority over people. The sense then becomes: if your ambitions were satisfied and the affairs of the world were entrusted to you *while you are morally unhealthy*, you would cause corruption in the land and cut off the ties of kinship and relationship. A heart that flinches at cost is not a heart to be handed power.

Both readings converge on one truth: a man who will not carry the burden of obedience will not, in the end, be a source of good on the earth.

## Why kinship, of all things?

Ibn Kathir observes that the ayah pairs a general prohibition — spreading corruption on earth — with a specific one: severing the ties of kinship. Allah has commanded people to establish righteousness on earth *and* to join the ties of kinship by treating relatives well "in speech, actions, and spending wealth in charity."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word: **arḥām** is the plural of **raḥim**, the womb — the receptacle in the mother where the unborn child is conceived, held, protected and developed before birth. Because that is the source of all relationships and kinship, the word came to be used idiomatically for human relationship and kinship itself. So when the Qur'an says "you would cut your *arḥām*," it is naming the very thing that made you.

Ibn Kathir gathers a remarkable cluster of hadith here — because, in his words, "many authentic and sound Hadiths have been reported through numerous routes of transmission" on this.

**Al-Bukhari** recorded from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said that after Allah completed creating the creation, the womb stood up and pulled at the lower garment of the Most Merciful. He said, "Stop that!" It replied, "My stand here is the stand of one seeking refuge in You from severance of ties." Allah said, "Would it not please you that I join whoever joins you and sever whoever severs you?" It replied, "Yes indeed!" He said, "You are granted that!" Abu Hurayrah then added: *Read if you wish* — and recited our ayah 22. Al-Bukhari also recorded another wording in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself said, "Read if you wish," and recited the ayah; Muslim also recorded it. That a Companion, and the Prophet ﷺ himself, cited *this* verse for kinship tells you the verse is no passing aside — it is a foundation text for the rights of relatives.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger ﷺ said: "No sin deserves that Allah hasten its punishment in the worldly life, in addition to what He reserves in the Hereafter for those who commit it, more than injustice and severance of the ties of kinship." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "This Hadith is Sahih."

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from Thawban, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever likes for his life to be extended, and his provision increased, let him connect his ties of kinship." Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in recording this narration, but that it has a supporting narration in the Sahih.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger ﷺ said: "Verily, the womb is attached to the Throne. And connecting its ties does not mean dealing evenly with the kinsfolk, but it rather means that if one's kinsfolk sever the ties, he connects them." Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari also recorded it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from Bukhari as well. This is the hardest and most useful line in the cluster. Repaying warmth with warmth is an exchange, not really a joining. The one who truly joins is the one who keeps reaching toward the relative who has cut him off.

**Ahmad** also recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr that the womb will be placed on the Day of Resurrection, curved like a spinning wheel, speaking with an eloquent, fluent tongue — severing whoever had severed it, and joining whoever had joined it.

And **Imam Ahmad** recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr that the Messenger ﷺ said: "The merciful ones will be granted mercy from the Most Merciful. Have mercy on those on earth — the One above the heavens will then have mercy on you. And *ar-raḥim* (the womb) is from *ar-Raḥmān*, so whoever joins it, it joins him; and whoever severs it, it severs him." Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi both recorded it, that it has been reported with continuous chains of transmission, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih." The hadith itself states the link: the womb is from the Most Merciful. To cut kinship is to set yourself against something the Prophet ﷺ traced back to the name of *ar-Raḥmān* Himself.

## The verdict

"Such are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has made them deaf and blinded their vision."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the curse plainly: people who cause corruption in the land and break the bonds of kinship have been cursed by Allah — that is, He has **driven them away from His mercy**. This is where the passage lands, and it is the same people it began with: those who recoiled when the command came, whose fear showed in their faces, and who would have found obedience better for them had they been true to Allah.

## Two rulings the scholars drew from these ayat

**The sale of *umm al-walad*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that on the basis of ayah 23, Sayyidnā ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, regarded the sale of an *umm al-walad* as unlawful. *Umm al-walad* is the term used in Islamic law for a bondwoman who has borne a child to her master and who is consequently free at his death. Selling the mother would separate the child from her, and that would sever the kinship tie between mother and child — which, as this verse says, brings the curse of Allah. The reasoning shows how seriously the earliest generation took the verse: it was strong enough to settle a question of law.

**Cursing a named individual.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when ʿAbdullah asked his father Imam Ahmad about cursing Yazid, the Imam answered, "Why should we not curse a person whom Allah has cursed in the Qur'an?" ʿAbdullah said he had read the Qur'an in its entirety and had not found Yazid cursed anywhere; his father recited this very verse and said, who could be worse than Yazid in breaking up relationships — he did not even care for the relations of the Prophet ﷺ. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to add that **the majority of the Ummah hold that it is not permissible to curse any particular person** unless we know for sure that he died in the state of disbelief. What may be used is a cursing phrase with general characteristics: the curse of Allah be upon the liars, upon the mischief-makers, upon the breaker of kinship. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, it notes, discusses the issue elaborately. This is a genuine difference among scholars, and the majority's path is the safer one to walk.

## Living it

Most of us will never face the test these ayat describe in its original form. But the anatomy is exactly the same, and it lands in ordinary life:

- **The gap between wanting a duty and doing it.** It is easy to admire commitment in the abstract. Ayah 21 locates the truth of a person at the moment "the matter is resolved" — when, as Ibn Kathir says, the situation becomes serious and the time truly arrives.
- **Sincerity is the whole currency.** "If they had been true to Allah" — Ibn Kathir reads this as making the intention sincerely for Him. Before the deed, check the intention; that is where truthfulness with Allah is decided.
- **The relative who cut you off.** By the hadith Ibn Kathir cites, the one who joins ties is not the one who deals evenly, returning kindness for kindness, but the one who connects them when his kinsfolk have severed them. That is a concrete, uncomfortable, doable action this week.
- **Kinship is spoken, done, and spent.** Ibn Kathir specifies three currencies: speech, actions, and spending wealth in charity. A message, a visit, and something from your pocket.
- **Fear, left unaddressed, hardens.** What ayah 20 records about these men is fear, terror and cowardice — and what ayah 23 records is that they were driven away from Allah's mercy, made deaf and blind. Between the two lies a refusal that could have been an obedience.

passages.title: Locked hearts and those who relapse into disbelief
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat trace a single downward path: a heart that will not open to the Qur'an, a person who then turns back after the truth had already become clear, a secret arrangement with those who hate what Allah revealed, and finally the moment of death when the angels come. Twice the passage stops to name a reason with the same phrase — **"that is because…"** (ayat 26 and 28). The Qur'an is not only describing an outcome; it is naming what produced it.

## Ayah 24 — the question that is really an instruction

*"Do they not then reflect on the Qur'an? Or are there locks upon their hearts?"*

Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah by saying that here Allah is **commanding the people to reflect and ponder upon the Qur'an, and prohibiting them from turning away from it**. So the first thing to notice is that the sentence is a question in form but a command in force. The Qur'an was not sent to be recited past; it was sent to be entered.

The Arabic verb is *yatadabbarūn*, from *tadabbur* — which Ibn Kathir renders as reflecting and pondering upon the Qur'an. It asks for the kind of attention that stops at a phrase and stays there.

Then comes the alternative: *am ʿalā qulūbin aqfāluhā* — "or upon hearts are their locks?" *Aqfāl* is the Arabic word for locks. Ibn Kathir's comment on the phrase is stark: it **"means, there indeed are locks upon some hearts, firmly closing them so that none of its meanings can reach them."** Note the force of his wording — not a door left ajar, but a fastening that shuts the heart so completely that the meanings of the Qur'an cannot get in at all.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this image in its Qur'anic family: the meaning of the phrase is **synonymous with similar phrases in other verses where words like *khatm* or *ṭabʿ*** — that Allah "has set a seal" on their hearts — are used. And it explains what such language describes: **the disbelievers refuse to employ their hearts for the comprehension of truth, and as a natural consequence their capacities to distinguish right from wrong have become atrophied.** Then it names the cause plainly: **"Carelessly committing sins all the time is the main cause of this. Allah forbid!"**

That last sentence deserves to be sat with. On this explanation the lock is not arbitrary. *Atrophied* is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own word, and it is the word of a faculty that wastes because it is never used — the refusal comes first, and the withering follows.

## The young man from Yemen

Ibn Kathir preserves a scene that turns this ayah from a warning into a door left ajar. **Ibn Jarir recorded from Hisham bin ʿUrwah, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ once recited this ayah** — *"Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?"* — **and a young man from Yemen said: "Indeed, there are locks upon them — until Allah opens them totally or slightly."**

That young man did in the moment exactly what the ayah demands: he heard the recitation and reflected, and the reflection produced an answer that neither denied the locks nor despaired of them. Yes, there are locks — and there is One who opens them. Total opening or slight opening, both are His to give.

Ibn Kathir then records what followed: **after that, ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, always liked that young man, and kept that to himself until he became in charge, upon which he utilised him** as a consultant. A single reflective sentence from an unknown youth left a mark, and when ʿUmar came to authority he put that young man to use. It says something about how the Companions valued *tadabbur*: a person who could genuinely think with the Qur'an was worth keeping close.

And it says something about what to do with a heart that feels shut. The young man's phrasing is a supplication in disguise. If the lock is Allah's to open, then the response to spiritual dullness is not resignation but asking — and returning to the recitation rather than turning away from it, which is precisely what this ayah prohibits.

## Ayah 25 — turning back

*"Indeed, those who relapse ˹into disbelief˺ after ˹true˺ guidance had become clear to them…"*

The Arabic is *irtaddū ʿalā adbārihim* — they turned back. Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: **"they departed from the faith and returned to disbelief."**

The aggravating clause is *min baʿdi mā tabayyana lahumu'l-hudā* — "after guidance had become clear to them." This is not the failure of someone who never saw. The guidance had already become clear; the turning came afterwards.

**Two moves of Shayṭān.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the fact that in this one sentence **two acts have been ascribed to the devil**:

- *Taswīl* — **"the act of decking out evil works fair to some people."** Ibn Kathir says the same of this word: **"he adorned and beautified that (apostasy) for them."** Shayṭān does not usually sell a person ugliness. He re-labels it.
- *Imlāʾ* — **"the act of giving respite."** Ibn Kathir renders the phrase *"filled them with false hopes… he tempted them, and deceived them."*

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the order: **first he made their evil works look good and beautiful to them, and then prolonged their false hopes which will never be fulfilled.**

That sequence is worth holding onto. Step one makes the wrong thing look attractive; step two supplies hopes that, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, will never be fulfilled — the sense that there is still time, that the matter can be settled later. The first move gets a person to act; the second is what keeps him there.

## Ayah 26 — "we will obey you in part of the matter"

*"That is because they said ˹privately˺ to those who ˹also˺ detest what Allah has revealed: 'We will obey you in part of the matter.' And Allah knows their secrets."*

Here the ayah pulls back the curtain and shows what was going on beneath the surface. Ibn Kathir explains the words *sanuṭīʿukum fī baʿḍi'l-amr* — "we will obey you in part of the matter" — as meaning that **they plotted secretly with them and gave them evil advice, as is the common practice of the hypocrites, who declare the opposite of what they conceal.**

Two details carry the weight.

**"To those who hate what Allah has sent down."** The partners in this arrangement are identified by exactly that: their hatred of what Allah revealed. That is the ground the alliance stands on.

**"In part of the matter."** Not everything — a portion. The Qur'an records the promise in their own words, and the phrase *"that is because"* presents this as the reason for the condemnation just pronounced.

**And Allah knows their secrets.** The conversation was private, and it is reported in the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir: **"whatever they hide and conceal, Allah is well-acquainted with it and He knows it,"** and he pairs it with the ayah *"And Allah records all that they plot by night"* (4:81). Allah's knowledge is affirmed here as it is stated: reaching what is hidden and what is concealed. The whole logic of hypocrisy — that the outward face is what counts because the inner one goes unseen — has nothing to stand on once that is true.

## Ayah 27 — "then how will it be…?"

*"Then how ˹horrible˺ will it be when the angels take their souls, striking their faces and their backs?"*

The sentence deliberately does not finish. *Fa-kayfa* — "then how…?" — leaves the reader to supply the answer, and nothing the reader supplies is adequate. The scene of the secret conversation is cut off and replaced with the moment none of it had accounted for.

Ibn Kathir describes it: **"how their situation will be when the angels come to take their lives, and their souls cling to their bodies, causing the angels to extract them by force, harshness, and beating."** The soul does not go willingly. It clings, and it is taken anyway.

He anchors the image in two parallel passages. *"If you could but see when the angels take away the lives of the disbelievers, striking their faces and their backs"* (8:50). And *"If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, while the angels extend their hands"* (6:93) — Ibn Kathir notes that extending the hands here means **to beat them** — with the words that follow: *"Deliver your souls! This day you will be recompensed with the torment of degradation because of what you used to utter against Allah other than the truth, and because you used to arrogantly reject His signs"* (6:93).

Notice what that recompense is called: *ʿadhāb al-hūn*, **the torment of degradation**. And notice what the same ayah gives as its cause — speaking against Allah other than the truth, and arrogantly rejecting His signs. The ayah itself sets the humiliation opposite the arrogance.

## Ayah 28 — the reason, stated plainly

*"This is because they follow whatever displeases Allah and hate what earns His pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless."*

The passage closes by naming the matter in the simplest terms, and what it names is not a failure of information but of wanting. Two verbs describe them: they **followed** what angered Allah, and they **hated** what earns His pleasure. Their pursuit was pointed one way and their aversion the other.

*Fa-aḥbaṭa aʿmālahum* — **"so He rendered their deeds worthless."** That is the stated end of it.

## Living it

**Read to be changed, not merely to finish.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 24 as a command to reflect and ponder upon the Qur'an, and a prohibition against turning away from it. Both halves are worth taking personally.

**Take dullness of heart seriously, and treat its cause.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces this hardening to carelessly committing sins all the time. Where the heart has gone dull, the repair begins where the dulling began.

**Ask for the opening.** The young man of Yemen said the locks remain **until Allah opens them totally or slightly**. Both are His to give, and both can be asked for.

**Learn Shayṭān's two moves.** *Taswīl* is when something wrong starts to look good and beautiful. *Imlāʾ* is the respite — the prolonged hope that will never be fulfilled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives them in that order, and the order is worth remembering.

**Watch the "small" concession.** They promised obedience only *"in part of the matter"* — and the Qur'an records the sentence and names it as the reason for what follows.

**Live as though the private room has a witness — because it does.** *"And Allah knows their secrets."* Whatever is hidden and concealed, Ibn Kathir says, Allah is well-acquainted with it and He knows it.

passages.title: Hidden malice exposed by trial
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are about a hidden thing and how it comes to light. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān says this verse was revealed in connection with the hypocrites, to expose the bitter hatred and rancour against Islam that they were hiding in their hearts: outwardly they expressed their love for the Holy Prophet ﷺ, while inwardly they harboured violent hatred and enmity for him. Ayah 29 asks them a stinging question: did they really imagine that what they had buried would stay buried? Ayah 30 answers that Allah could have named every one of them outright, but chose not to — while still leaving them detectable in the way they talk. Ayah 31 then reveals the mechanism by which the sorting actually happens: trial. Commands, prohibitions, and the hard demands of struggle and patience shake the community until what is inside each person shows on the outside.

So the unit moves in a straight line: **the concealed malice (29) → Allah's decision to veil it while giving His Prophet ﷺ a way to sense it (30) → the testing that separates the sincere from the pretender (31).**

## "Those in whose hearts is a disease"

The passage does not open by naming the hypocrites. It describes them by a symptom: *fī qulūbihim maraḍ* — "in whose hearts is a disease." What is diseased is the heart itself, not the outward profession; as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān puts it, the love was on the outside and the enmity was within.

Ibn Kathir reads the question in ayah 29 as directed straight at them: do the hypocrites think that Allah will not expose their affair to His believing servant? And he answers — yes indeed, He will expose their affair and manifest it, so that those with insight will be able to understand it.

He points to how this actually happened. Allah revealed Sūrah Barā'ah (also called At-Tawbah), in which He clarified the hypocrites' scandals and pinpointed their practices that are indicative of their hypocrisy. Because of that, Ibn Kathir notes, that sūrah is also called **"The Exposer"** (Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives the Arabic name *fāḍiḥah*, meaning "exposing to shame or disgrace," because the specific qualities of the hypocrites are set out in it). So the threat of ayah 29 is not abstract. A whole sūrah of the Qur'an is its fulfilment.

## Aḍghān: the word for a buried grudge

Everything in ayah 29 hangs on one word: *aḍghān*.

Ibn Kathir explains that *aḍghān* is the plural of *ḍighn*, which means **what the souls harbour of envy and hatred toward Islam and toward its people who support it**. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives the same range: secret enmity, rancour, malice, spite.

Notice what the word carries in itself: it is something *hidden*. A *ḍighn* is not an argument you have out with someone; it is what a soul harbours, and what the two commentaries both describe as *secret*.

Notice too the verb: *an lan yukhrija Allāhu aḍghānahum* — that Allah will never **bring out** their grudges. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sharpens the irony of their position: these people knew that Allah is the Knower of the unseen, yet they were not concerned that He would expose their inner secret and covert enmity to the people. They believed enough to know they were being watched, and lived as though they were not.

## Ayah 30: the naming that Allah withheld

*"Had We so willed, We could have shown them clearly to you, so that you would know them by their marks."*

Ibn Kathir paraphrases Allah addressing His Messenger ﷺ: had We willed, O Muhammad, We would have shown you the specific individuals who are hypocrites, so that you would plainly know them.

But — and this is the heart of the ayah — Allah did not do that in regard to all of the hypocrites. Ibn Kathir's words on this are among the most beautiful in the passage: **Allah conceals His creation, lets their affairs run according to apparent purity, and leaves the inner secrets to the One Who is well aware of them.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws attention to the grammar. The clause is introduced by *law* ("if"), the Arabic hypothetical particle; introduced that way, the sentence implies that what is supposed either does not occur or is not likely to take place. So the very structure of the sentence tells you the showing did not happen. And it explains the wisdom: Allah's wisdom and clemency did not wish to expose them to shame and disgrace in this way, and so the principle was maintained that **all worldly matters be decided by their outer appearance, and the inner conditions and matters of the heart be left to the All-Knowing Allah.**

This is a foundational principle of how the believing community is meant to function. A person whose outward affairs are sound is dealt with on that basis — his heart is Allah's business, not ours. The alternative — a community where everyone's inner state is public — was available to Allah, and He deliberately declined it. Any of us who has ever wished he could see straight through people should sit with that.

## Laḥn al-qawl: what the tongue gives away

Having withheld the list of names, ayah 30 immediately grants something else: *wa la-taʿrifannahum fī laḥn al-qawl* — "but you will know them by the tone of their speech."

Ibn Kathir explains this as: you will know them by their speech that reveals their intentions. A person declares his association through the context and meaning of his words. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān puts it as an insight Allah gave the Holy Prophet ﷺ, by which he was able to perceive the inner nature and real character of the hypocrites by the *style* of their speech.

So what Allah left His Prophet ﷺ was not a list but a manner: not the names of the men, but the tone of the talk.

Both commentaries quote the Commander of the Faithful **ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him)**: *"Never would one conceal a secret but Allah will expose it by the look on his face and the uncontrolled words of his tongue."* Maʿārif renders it: anyone who conceals a secret in his heart, Allah displays it on his face and brings it out by the slip of his tongue — in the course of conversation, some such words slip out which express the inner secret.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān also reports a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ to the effect that when a person harbours a secret thought in his heart, Allah puts a cover on it — and if it is good, it becomes manifest. (The source cites this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here as a teaching, not attributed to a named book.)

And it should be added that the withholding in ayah 30 was not total. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that some narrations of ahadith describe the Holy Prophet ﷺ being imparted the knowledge of a group of the hypocrites by name. It records, on the authority of **ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr (may Allah be pleased with him), in the *Musnad* of Imam Ahmad**, that the Holy Prophet ﷺ in one of his sermons called out the names of particular hypocrites and asked them to leave the congregation — thirty-six names counted altogether. (Maʿārif attributes the report to Ibn Kathir.) So Allah showed him some, and veiled the rest.

Ayah 30 then closes with a line that hangs over the whole passage: *"And Allah knows all your deeds."* No one — hypocrite or believer — is operating unobserved.

## Ayah 31: the trial that sorts

*"And We will surely try you, until We know those who strive among you and the patient, and We will put to a test all your affairs."*

Ibn Kathir explains *wa la-nabluwannakum* — "And We will surely try you" — as: **We will surely test you with commands and prohibitions.** That is worth pausing on. The testing instrument named here is the ordinary machinery of the religion — being told to do things and being told to stop doing things. Every command is a place where the sincere and the resentful part company, because obedience costs something.

Two qualities are named as what the test brings out: *al-mujāhidīn* — those who strive — and *al-ṣābirīn* — the patient. The first is active effort, the second is holding steady; between them they cover what a hard road demands.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains the purpose in context: Allah has enjoined fighting on the believers so that sincere believers may become distinguished from the hypocrites, who shrink in horror at the very thought of fighting. This connects the passage back to ayah 29. A man can conceal a *ḍighn* indefinitely while nothing is asked of him. He cannot conceal it when the call goes out and there is a cost to answering. The trial does not create the difference; it makes an existing difference visible.

The final phrase, *wa nabluwa akhbārakum* — "and We will put to a test all your affairs" — widens the scope: not one moment of testing, but the whole of a person's affairs put to the test.

## "Until We know" — a note on Allah's knowledge

The phrase *ḥattā naʿlama* ("until We know") has to be understood carefully, and both commentaries stop to do so.

Ibn Kathir states it plainly: **there is absolutely no doubt that Allah's knowledge precedes the occurrence of all events.** Nothing happens that Allah did not already know. In this ayah, "until We know" means *until We know of its occurrence*. He cites **Ibn ʿAbbās** on this and similar texts: *"'Except so that We may know' means, so that We may see."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān frames the same point in terms of two kinds of knowledge: knowledge of a thing *before* its occurrence, and knowledge of a thing *after* it has actually happened. Allah's knowledge of things is since eternity; the knowledge referred to in this ayah is of the second kind — knowledge of things after the occurrence of the events in the external world.

In other words, the ayah is not saying Allah learns something. It is saying the test brings the deed out into the external world, where it has actually occurred. Allah knew who would strive; the trial is what turns that eternal knowledge into a striver who has, in fact, striven.

## Living it

**Stop auditing other people's hearts.** Ayah 30 is Allah telling His own Prophet ﷺ that He did not hand him the full list. Allah conceals His creation and lets their affairs run according to apparent purity. If that restraint was built into the Prophet's ﷺ own situation, our suspicion of one another's inner states has no standing at all. Worldly matters are decided by their outer appearance; the matters of the heart are left to the All-Knowing Allah.

**Audit your own.** *Aḍghān* is what a soul harbours of envy and hatred — something its owner can carry without ever saying it out loud. The question of ayah 29 belongs to every one of us before it belongs to anyone else: what am I storing that I would not want brought out?

**Listen to your own tone.** ʿUthmān's observation (may Allah be pleased with him) cuts both ways. If a concealed secret is displayed on the face and brought out by the slip of the tongue, then the way we speak about Allah's commands is data about our hearts that we did not consciously choose to publish.

**Expect the sorting.** Ayah 31 says the test is coming, and Ibn Kathir tells us the ordinary form it takes: commands and prohibitions. Every instruction of the religion that you find heavy is a place where your true position is being brought into the open. Better to be sorted here, where the outcome can still be changed, than to have gone through life with a disease no one — including yourself — ever named.

passages.title: Do not nullify your deeds or sue for peace
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set two kinds of loss side by side. The enemies of the message lose everything they ever built (ayat 32 and 34), and the believers are warned that they too can lose what they have built — not by the swords of others, but by their own hands (ayah 33) — before the passage closes by telling them that if they hold their nerve, nothing they have done will ever be lost at all (ayah 35).

That is the thread: **deeds, and what happens to them.** The word *ʿamal* — action, work, deed — runs through every ayah of the passage. In ayah 32 Allah will render the disbelievers' deeds vain. In ayah 33 the believers are told not to render their own deeds vain. In ayah 35 they are promised that Allah **will never deprive them** of their deeds. Read as one unit, the passage is a lesson in how a lifetime of work can be preserved or destroyed, and it ends by joining that inner question — the integrity of your deeds — to an outer one: how a community behaves toward its enemies when it holds the stronger hand.

## Ayah 32 — three things they did, and the one thing they could not do

Ayah 32 stacks three charges. They **disbelieved**; they **hindered others from the path of Allah**; and they **opposed the Messenger ﷺ** — Ibn Kathir's wording is that they oppose the Messenger ﷺ and contend with him. And all of this, the ayah adds, **after the guidance had been made clear to them**. Their rejection was not confusion. It was refusal with the light in front of them.

Ibn Kathir explains that this includes those who "revert from the faith after guidance has become clear to them" — apostasy after knowledge. And then comes the ayah's crushing verdict on such people: **they will not harm Allah in the least.** All that effort, all that organising and obstructing, does not scratch the One they are fighting. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: they only harm themselves and become losers on the Day of Resurrection.

**Who, historically?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the ayah also refers to the hypocrites, and to the Jewish tribes of Banū Qurayẓah and Banū Naḍīr. Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said it refers to those hypocrites who, on the occasion of the battle of Badr, joined forces with the disbelievers of Quraysh and helped them — twelve men of the two tribes taking upon themselves the responsibility of feeding the entire army, each taking his turn to organise the meals for the enemy camp on different days. Hold that image, because it is the point of the ayah: that is a real, costly, generous effort. Twelve men feeding an army is not nothing. And the ayah's answer is that it will be blown away.

## "He will render their deeds vain" — two ways to read it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *ḥabṭ al-aʿmāl* (the rendering of deeds vain) here carries either of two meanings, and both fit:

1. **Their campaign fails.** Their efforts to undermine Islam come to nothing.
2. **Their good works are void.** Because of their disbelief and hypocrisy, the charity they gave, the free-will offerings, the philanthropic activity — none of it will be accepted.

Ibn Kathir presses the second point hard. Allah will not reward them "even the weight of a mosquito" for any good they did before their apostasy; it is totally invalidated and destroyed. Then he gives the image that makes it land: **their apostasy wipes away their good deeds entirely, just as good deeds would normally wipe away evil deeds.** The eraser works in both directions. What we hope righteousness will do to our sins, disbelief does to our righteousness.

## Ayah 33 — the warning turns inward

Then the address changes: **"O you who believe! Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger, and do not invalidate your deeds."** Having shown the believers the wreckage of other people's life's work, Allah turns and says: this can happen to you too.

Ibn Kathir reads the command to obedience as what results in the believers' happiness in this worldly life and the Hereafter, and reads **"do not invalidate your deeds"** as a prohibition of apostasy — because apostasy is precisely what results in the nullification of deeds, as the very next ayah confirms.

**A precise word-choice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to miss. Of the disbelievers, ayah 32 used *ḥabṭ al-aʿmāl*. But to the believers in ayah 33, the Qurʼan says *lā tubṭilū aʿmālakum* — *ibṭāl al-aʿmāl*. The change of word is deliberate, because **the scope of *ibṭāl* is much wider than *ḥabṭ***. It covers two distinct cases:

- **Nullification by disbelief.** No action of a die-hard disbeliever is ever acceptable. And if someone embraced Islam and later abandoned it, the good works done during his days of Islam — works that were genuinely acceptable at the time — are made vain by the disbelief and apostasy that followed.
- **Nullification by failing a condition.** The acceptability of some righteous deeds is conditional upon other righteous acts. If the condition is not fulfilled, the deed is rendered fruitless.

That second category is where this ayah reaches into an ordinary believing life.

## What can quietly cancel a deed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds the second category in the Qurʼan itself. The necessary condition for every righteous action is that it be **performed exclusively and sincerely for Allah**, and not as an ostentatious display to people: *"They were commanded only to worship Allah, making their submission sincere for Him"* (98:5), and *"Unquestionably, for Allah is the pure religion"* (39:3). And a deed can be undone after it is done: *"O you who believe, do not nullify your charities by boasting about favour, and teasing"* (2:264) — give charity to a needy person and then follow it up with demands of gratitude or insulting words, and you have nullified the charitable act itself.

The early authorities read our ayah along exactly these lines. **Ibn Jurayj** explained it as: do not nullify your virtuous acts by doing them only to show off and to win a good name among the people. **Muqātil and others** explained it as *bil-mann* — do not nullify your deeds by boasting about the favour you did.

**A statement that needs careful handling.** **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** (may Allah have mercy on him) explained the ayah as: *"Do not render vain your own good works by means of sins."* Taken at face value that would mean any sin nullifies all good deeds — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say that this apparent sense is against the well-established position, so it cannot be what he meant. Two ways of understanding him are offered:

- He refers only to those sins that are relevant to a particular virtuous act and that nullify **that act alone** — as *riyāʼ* (ostentation, showing off) must be avoided for a good work to be accepted.
- Or he refers to the **deprivation of the blessing** of righteous works rather than their outright nullification: if a believer's sins are much more than his good deeds, the few good deeds he has to his credit will be devoid of the blessing that might have saved him from the punishment of his sins. By the rule of retribution he is punished first for his sins, and finally, through the virtue of his faith, he attains salvation and is admitted into the gardens of Paradise.

**The settled Sunni position**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it: according to the unanimity of *ahl al-sunnah wa'l-jamāʿah*, **no sin — not even a major sin other than *kufr* or *shirk* — can destroy the righteous acts of a believer.** If a believer who prays regularly and keeps his fasts were to steal something, the sacred law does not declare his prayers and fasts null and void, nor demand that he repeat them.

## Why the Companions were frightened

Ibn Kathir preserves two reports that show what this ayah did to the first generation.

**Imam Aḥmad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī reported in *Kitāb aṣ-Ṣalāh* (the Book of Prayer)** that Abu al-ʿĀliyah said: the Prophet's ﷺ Companions used to think that no sin would harm a person who says *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, just as no good deed would benefit a person who joins partners with Allah. Then Allah revealed *"Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds"* — **and this made them fear that some sins could nullify their deeds.**

And it is reported from **Ibn ʿUmar** (may Allah be pleased with him): "We, the Companions of Allah's Messenger ﷺ, used to think that good deeds would all be accepted, until Allah revealed *'Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds.'* So we asked each other: 'What is it that can nullify our deeds?' So we said, 'The major sins, great offences that require admission into the Fire and immoral sins.'" But then Allah revealed **"Verily, Allah does not forgive joining partners with Him in worship, but He forgives except that to whom He wills"** (4:48). Ibn ʿUmar continues: "After this was revealed, we ceased saying that. We thereafter continued to fear for those who committed great sins and immoral sins and to have hope for those who did not."

That last line is worth sitting with. Revelation did not remove their fear; it **calibrated** it. They stopped declaring that major sins wipe out a lifetime of worship, and settled into the believer's proper posture — fear for the sinner without despair, hope for the obedient without complacency.

## A juristic dispute the ayah generates

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference of the jurists arising from the generality of *lā tubṭilū aʿmālakum*. If a believer begins a *nafl* — an act of worship that is not obligatory — and then deliberately disrupts it before its completion:

- **Imam Abū Ḥanīfah** deems this to be nullifying the deed, and holds it impermissible. On this reading, once a person commences a righteous act that was not initially obligatory, its completion becomes obligatory; whoever breaks it off without a legitimate reason, or nullifies it purposely, is a sinner, and it is obligatory for him to make *qaḍāʼ* (to make it up). The Ḥanafī argument is that the wording of this ayah is general in scope, embracing all righteous acts, obligatory and supererogatory alike.
- **Imam Shāfiʿī** holds that he is neither a sinner nor obliged to make *qaḍāʼ*, his argument being that the act was not initially obligatory, so its abandonment does not entail a sin.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that on this occasion Tafsīr Maẓharī quotes a large number of narrations and discusses the issue in detail. Both positions are the reasoning of great imams; a believer follows the school he follows without condemning the other.

## Ayah 34 — why the warning is repeated

Ayah 34 sounds almost like ayah 32 again: those who disbelieved and obstructed others from the path of Allah, **"and then died as disbelievers — never will Allah forgive them."** Why repeat it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two answers:

- Ayah 32 describes their loss **in this world**; ayah 34 describes their loss **in the next**.
- Or: ayah 32 spoke of disbelievers **in general**, including those who would later embrace Islam — the ruling for them being that the good works done in the state of disbelief go to waste and will not be rewarded even after they enter Islam. Ayah 34 refers in particular to those who **persisted in their disbelief until their dying day**; the ruling for them is that Allah will never forgive them in the next world. And Allah knows best.

The decisive words are *thumma mātū wa hum kuffār* — **"and then died as disbelievers."** As long as a person breathes, the door is open. It is death upon disbelief that closes it. Ibn Kathir links this to 4:48: shirk is the one sin excluded from the scope of forgiveness; everything below it lies within Allah's will to forgive.

## Ayah 35 — do not go weak, and do not beg

The passage ends by turning the same principle outward: **"So do not lose heart and beg for peace while you are superior. Allah is with you, and He will never deprive you of your deeds."**

**"Do not lose heart"** — *fa-lā tahinū*. Ibn Kathir: do not be weak concerning the enemies. **"And beg for peace"** — *tadʿū ilā al-salm* — Ibn Kathir explains as compromise, peace, and ending the fighting between you and the disbelievers **while you are in a position of power, both in great numbers and in preparations**. And *wa antum al-aʿlawn*, "while you are superior," states the condition exactly: the prohibition attaches to **the condition of your superiority over your enemy**.

**When a treaty is right.** Ibn Kathir immediately gives the other side. If, on the other hand, the disbelievers are considered more powerful and numerous than the Muslims, the Imam — the general commander — may decide to hold a treaty if he judges that it entails a benefit for the Muslims. And he cites the Prophet's ﷺ own precedent: when the disbelievers obstructed him from entering Makkah and offered him a treaty in which all fighting would stop between them for ten years, **he ﷺ agreed to that.** The one who was commanded not to sue for peace out of weakness is the same one who accepted that ten-year truce. The difference is not between war and peace; it is between **strategy and a collapse of nerve.**

**Reconciling two ayat.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: this ayah prohibits the Muslims from inviting the disbelievers into a peace treaty, yet elsewhere Allah says *"And if they tilt towards peace, tilt towards it"* (8:61), which indicates that if the disbelievers want peace it is permissible to enter into a peace agreement with them. Some scholars therefore held that the permission is conditional upon the disbelievers taking the initiative in peace negotiations, while our ayah prohibits the Muslims from taking that initiative — on which reading there is no conflict between the two ayat.

**But the authentic ruling**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, is that **it is permissible for Muslims even to take the initiative in negotiating peace, if it could be in the best interest of the Muslims** — *not* by reason of cowardice and involvement in a life of luxury. The key is the wording of the ayah itself: by employing *fa-lā tahinū*, "do not lose heart," the Qurʼan indicates that what is prohibited is **an appeal for peace based on cowardice and escaping from jihād**. On this reading too there is no conflict between the two ayat, since inclining to peace is restricted to a situation where it rests on the interest of the Muslims, and not on cowardice or leisure. And Allah knows best.

## "Allah is with you"

Two promises close the passage, and they are the answer to everything the passage has raised.

**"And Allah is with you."** Ibn Kathir: this contains the good news of victory and triumph over the enemies. It is said to a community that has just been told not to flinch.

**"And He will never deprive you of your deeds"** — *wa lan yatirakum aʿmālakum*. Ibn Kathir: Allah will never invalidate your deeds, nullify them, or deprive you of them; **rather He will give you your rewards complete, without any reduction.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the consolation that follows from it: Allah will not diminish the reward of the believers, so if they suffer any pain or loss in this world they will receive a huge reward in the next — and therefore **a believer is never unsuccessful, even in the face of pain or difficulty.**

Notice how exactly this answers ayah 33. There the believers were warned, *do not invalidate your deeds*; here they are assured, *Allah will never invalidate your deeds.* The only thing that can destroy your record is you. Allah will not cheat you of a single act.

## Living it

- **The danger to your deeds is internal.** No enemy in ayah 32, for all his organisation, can take a single deed from you. The passage's warning about losing your work is addressed to *believers*, about their own conduct.
- **Guard the deed after you have done it.** 2:264, cited here, teaches that a completed charity can still be nullified afterwards by boasting about the favour and wounding the one you helped. Ibn Jurayj and Muqātil read our ayah the same way. A deed is not safe the moment it is finished.
- **Fear without despair.** The Companions' reaction to this ayah, and its correction by 4:48, is the model: take your sins seriously enough to fear for yourself, while knowing that short of shirk nothing places you beyond Allah's forgiveness, and that no such sin cancels a believer's prayers and fasts.
- **Finish what you start.** Whatever one's school on the ruling, the spirit of Abū Ḥanīfah's reading is sound counsel: a voluntary act of worship begun is worth completing rather than dropped halfway.
- **Know the difference between wisdom and weakness.** A truce concluded for the benefit of the Muslims is what the Prophet ﷺ himself did; a truce begged for out of cowardice and escaping from struggle, when you hold the upper hand, is what ayah 35 forbids. The ayah scrutinises the motive, not merely the outcome.

passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close sūrah 47 — Ibn Kathir signs off immediately after them with the words, "This concludes the Tafsir of Surat Al-Qital. And Allah is worthy of all praise and gratitude."

Ibn Kathir titles his comment on this passage "Showing the Triviality of the Worldly Life and encouraging Spending," and that title is the thread of the whole passage. Ayah 36 puts the world in its true size; ayat 37 and 38 then test the claim of faith at the exact point where it is most easily exposed — the wallet.

Laid out plainly: the world is small (36); Allah does not need anything from you (36, 38); He has asked only a little (37); yet even at that little, some hold back (38); and the loss of holding back falls on no one but the one who holds back (38).

## Why the world is put in its place *here*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection explicit. Muslims have been enjoined to fight in the cause of Allah, and for that they will have to make sacrifices of life and money. And "the love of this world is the only thing that can prevent man from fighting." So before the appeal to spend, Allah tells the truth about what is being clung to: neither of these worldly benefits is permanent. They will all perish and come to an end. Even if we succeed in saving them for now, they will be lost another time. The bounties of the next world, by contrast, are permanent and eternal — and it is *those* that the believers need to develop love for, not the perishable things of this passing world.

Read that way, ayah 36 is not a scolding. It is a kindness: Allah is loosening the grip of something that was going to be pulled from our hands anyway.

## Ayah 36: "only amusement and diversion"

**إِنَّمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا لَعِبٞ وَلَهۡوٞ** — "This worldly life is only amusement and diversion" (Ibn Kathir's rendering); "The worldly life is but play and pastime" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Ibn Kathir introduces the ayah as "expressing the insignificance and worthlessness of the worldly life."

But he immediately adds a qualification that changes everything, and it should not be skipped:

> "(This worldly life is only amusement and diversion) which means that such is its outcome, **except for that which is done for the sake of Allah**."

So the verdict is not on the world as a substance — not on wealth, work, family, or effort as such. It is on the *outcome*. Everything in this life resolves into amusement and diversion **except** the portion of it that was done for Allah's sake. That exception is the hinge on which the next two ayat turn: the way to rescue your worldly wealth from being mere amusement is to spend some of it for Allah.

**"And if you believe and have Taqwa of Allah, He will grant you your rewards, and will not ask from you (to sacrifice all of) your possessions."** *Taqwā* is the mindfulness of Allah that keeps a believer alert to Allah's watching and careful of His limits. Ibn Kathir explains the promise: "He is in no need of you, and asks you for nothing. He only ordained giving charity from your wealth so that you would help your needy brothers. The benefit of that would then come back to you, as well as the rewards."

Notice the direction of the flow. The charity leaves your hand, reaches a brother in need, and the benefit *returns* to you — twice over, once as the good done and once as the reward stored.

## A puzzle the scholars addressed: "and will not ask you your riches"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the difficulty honestly. The apparent meaning of the ayah is that Allah does not demand or urge you to hand over your wealth. Yet the Qur'an is replete with verses on zakāh, charities, and spending wealth in the way of Allah — and in the very next ayah the reader is emphatically called upon to spend in Allah's way. So there appears to be a conflict.

Two resolutions are recorded, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents them as the views of different scholars rather than settling the matter by force:

**First view.** Some scholars say the ayah means that Allah does not need their money for His benefit; it is for their own benefit that sacrifices of life and money are demanded. The evidence is in the same ayah: *yuʼtikum ujūrakum* — "He will give you your rewards." The believers are required to spend in Allah's way in a manner that will help them in the Hereafter, where they will need their righteous works most pressingly; that is where they will be rewarded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this interpretation was **preferred by Maulana Thanawi (raḥimahu Allāh)**, and points to a verse of identical meaning: *"I do not desire [to receive] any provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me"* (51:57).

**Second view.** Other scholars say that "asking your riches" means demanding *all* of one's wealth. Their argument is that this clause needs to be read in conjunction with ayah 37 — "If He were to ask you of it, and were to press you…" On this reading the general meaning of ayah 36 is restricted by ayah 37: what Allah does not ask for is the whole of your wealth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then sums the two ayat up together: the financial obligations Allah has imposed on the believers, such as zakāh, are for their own benefit; Allah does not need their money or wealth; and He has deliberately not demanded all of it, because that would be displeasing and a burden, and it would weigh heavily on us.

## Ayah 37: the pressure that would have exposed the heart

**إِن يَسۡـَٔلۡكُمُوهَا فَيُحۡفِكُمۡ تَبۡخَلُواْ وَيُخۡرِجۡ أَضۡغَٰنَكُمۡ**

The ayah works by describing a scenario that Allah, in His mercy, did not put us through.

**Yuḥfi** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word is derived from *iḥfāʼ*, which means "to pursue a work persistently and insistently until it is accomplished." Ibn Kathir glosses the clause simply: "if He pressures you much, you would become stingy." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that all scholars agree on the sense of ayah 37: if Allah were to demand all of their wealth, they would become niggardly, and acting on such an injunction would displease them — and the displeasure would become visible at the time of expending.

**Adghān** — the plural of *dighn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as "secret malice, grudge or hatred." The ayah says such pressure would *expose* these — Ibn Kathir renders the clause "And He will expose your (secret) ill-wills."

Ibn Kathir cites **Qatādah**: "Allah knows that extracting wealth (i.e., money from people) brings about ill-wills." And Ibn Kathir affirms it with a line worth memorising:

> "Indeed, Qatādah has said the truth, because money is dear to the people, and they do not spend it except in things that are dearer to them than it."

That is the whole psychology of giving in one sentence. Nobody parts with money for something they value less than the money. So what you spend on is a statement of what you actually love — and what you refuse to spend on is a statement too.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail that turns the point into something you can catch in yourself: naturally, a man feels unhappy to part with all of his wealth, and even if he does not express that unhappiness openly, he would procrastinate at the time of payment — and the procrastination would disclose his unhappiness. Reluctance rarely announces itself; it just keeps finding a later date.

## The mercy hidden in the small percentages

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that if Allah had demanded all of people's wealth, they would be tight-fisted, and because of that tight-fistedness their hearts would harbour rancour, malice, and spite against spending in the cause of Allah — which would then be exposed. So instead, through His grace and compassion, He imposed a nominal percentage:

- **Zakāh: 1/40th — 2.5%**
- **Agricultural produce: 1/10th (10%) or 1/20th (5%)**
- **Livestock: one goat out of every hundred goats**

That is the shape of the divine demand: He has asked for so little of our wealth that we should discharge our obligation "readily and happily." And this is precisely what makes ayah 38 so pointed — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, He imposed only a small and nominal share, "but people are niggardly even in this case."

## Ayah 38: "Here you are…"

**هَٰٓأَنتُمۡ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ تُدۡعَوۡنَ لِتُنفِقُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ** — "Here you are now invited to spend in Allah's cause; but among you are those who withhold (stingily)." Ibn Kathir's gloss on those who withhold is blunt: "they refuse to spend." And note that the ayah does not say *all* of you refuse — *fa-minkum man yabkhal*, "among you are those who withhold."

**"And whoever acts stingily is but stingy toward himself."** Ibn Kathir: "he only reduces his own rewards, and the bad outcome of that will come back to him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in different words: any person practising miserliness will himself suffer the loss, because he will have to carry the burden of failing to fulfil his obligation and will thus be deprived of reward in the Hereafter.

This is the ayah's great reversal. Stinginess feels like protecting yourself. The Qur'an says you are withholding *from* yourself — the money you clutch is the money you fail to send ahead to the one place you will genuinely need it.

## "Allah is Al-Ghanī and you are the poor"

**وَٱللَّهُ ٱلۡغَنِيُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلۡفُقَرَآءُ**

Ibn Kathir explains *Al-Ghanī*, the Need-Free: "Allah is in need of nothing else, whereas everything is ever in need of Him." And *al-fuqarāʼ*, "the needy" — meaning needy "specifically of Him."

Then he makes a point about the nature of these two descriptions that is worth pausing on: the description of Allah as *Al-Ghanī*, in no need, "is a necessary description of Allah"; and the description of the creation as *faqr*, neediness, "is a necessary description for them that they cannot avoid." This is not a situation that could have been arranged differently. Richness is what Allah is; poverty is what we are.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion: Allah is free of want and beyond any need, while man is in need of the means of a comfortable subsistence — so "spending in the way of Allah is for man's own good and to fulfil his own needs." The beggar in this transaction is not the One being given to.

## "And if you turn away, He will replace you"

**وَإِن تَتَوَلَّوۡاْ يَسۡتَبۡدِلۡ قَوۡمًا غَيۡرَكُمۡ ثُمَّ لَا يَكُونُوٓاْ أَمۡثَٰلَكُم**

Ibn Kathir: "if you turn away" means turning away "from obeying Him and adhering to His Laws." And the replacement people "will not be like you" — meaning, "rather, they will be people who will listen to Him and obey His commands."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as the clearest statement of Allah's freedom from need — described "so lucidly that it brings to our mind the fact that let alone people's wealth, **He does not even need their existence**." If they stop acting upon His injunctions, He will bring another people who will not turn away, but will obey Him completely, for as long as Allah wants to maintain the religion of truth, Islam.

Who are they? The sources record early views without collapsing them into one:

- **Al-Hasan al-Basri (raḥimahu Allāh)** said the reference in this verse is to non-Arabs.
- **ʿIkrimah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu)** said the reference is to the Persians and the Romans.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates a moment among the Companions. **Abū Hurayrah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu)** reported that when Allah's Messenger ﷺ recited this ayah in the presence of the Companions, they asked him who those people were who would be brought in their place if they were to turn away from Allah's injunctions — people who would not turn away as they had. **Salmān al-Fārisī (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu)** was sitting among them. The Prophet ﷺ slapped his hand on Salmān's thigh and said that if faith — the religion of truth — were to go up to the Pleiades, "a man of Persian descent will acquire it from there and act upon it."

*(Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates this report without naming the collection it comes from, so it is given here exactly as the commentary gives it.)*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that **Shaykh Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī** wrote a book on the biography of Abū Ḥanīfah (raḥimahu Allāh) in which he identifies him and his disciples as the people referred to in that report, because no group among the Persians reached the high point of knowledge that Abū Ḥanīfah and his disciples reached.

## Living it

**Measure your wealth against the exception in ayah 36.** Ibn Kathir's qualification is the practical key to the whole passage: such is the outcome of this life *except for that which is done for the sake of Allah*. Every day, some portion of what passes through your hands can be moved from the first column into the second. That is the only part of it you keep.

**Watch the delay, not the intention.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's observation about procrastination is a diagnostic anyone can run on themselves. When the moment to give arrives and you find yourself deferring, re-checking, waiting for a better time — that hesitation is disclosing something no self-assessment will.

**Take the smallness of the demand as mercy, not as a floor to negotiate down from.** He asked for a fortieth, and He asked for so little precisely so that the obligation could be discharged readily and happily. Meeting a 2.5% obligation grudgingly misses the whole reason it was set at 2.5%.

**Give with the direction of the transaction clear in your mind.** Allah is *Al-Ghanī*, in need of nothing. You are the *faqīr*, needy of Him, and you are sending provisions ahead to where you will need them most. The needy brother receives, and — as Ibn Kathir says — the benefit comes back to you, with the rewards on top.

**And take the last clause seriously.** If a people turn away from obeying Him, He will bring others who listen and obey, for as long as Allah wills to maintain the religion of truth. That should produce neither despair nor complacency — only the resolve to be among those who answer when they are called.
